items.title: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
items.author: Jacob May
items.summary: I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?” These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark. But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo . I didn't experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized's 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home. items.title: Alex Karp put Palantir’s early sales team in the Mandarin Oriental instead of a Motel 6—at 10x the price
items.author: Steven John
items.summary: The old advice to dress for the job you want can apply to lodging, too—at least in the thinking of some enterprising executives. In its early days, Palantir Technologies put its young staffers up at a luxury Mandarin Oriental for sales trips instead of booking a budget chain like Motel 6. The call came from Alex Karp, Palantir’s cofounder and CEO, and the logic was simple: In enterprise sales, appearances can matter as much as the bottom line. Even companies that will someday be worth hundreds of billions often start out with a “fake it ’til you make it” mentality. Garry Tan, who was Palantir’s 10th employee and is now CEO of startup accelerator Y Combinator, shared the story in a May 2025 post on X : “Funny early Palantir story. We were doing some of our first sales meetings for Palantir and (team was all under 25 at the time) and were staying at the Mandarin Oriental. We said hey this is a startup! Why are we wasting money on this? Alex Karp said the people you’re selling to will ask you where you are staying. And we aren’t selling Motel 6 software. We are selling Mandarin Oriental software.” From long shot to a $386 billion company Karp’s bet on looking the part has aged well. P

items.title: How much will Anthropic be worth at IPO? New platforms like Polymarket offer early clues
items.author: Camila Grigera Naón
items.summary: Anthropic doesn’t start trading on Nasdaq until Thursday, but prediction markets are already taking bets on what the Claude maker will be worth at the end of its debut. A Polymarket contract tied to Anthropic’s closing market capitalization has drawn nearly $10 million in trading volume. The leading bet, with odds of around 43%, is that Anthropic finishes the day worth between $1.25 trillion and $1.5 trillion. A finish below $1.25 trillion isn’t far behind at roughly 35%, while the odds of topping $1.5 trillion are about 20%. On Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange specializing in perpetual futures , one contract put Anthropic’s implied valuation at roughly $1.7 trillion, according to CoinGecko data . The contract trades around the clock, letting traders bet on what the company is worth without buying a single share. The estimates come as Anthropic prepares to set the price for its initial public offering Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq a day later under the ticker symbol ANT. The Claude maker initially sought $70 to $78 a share. One day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop that halted departures across the nation, upending travel plans for more than 1.5 million passengers. Even more disruptions have cascaded throughout this week: yet another outage affected banking websites and apps run by financial giants including Wells Fargo and Capital One , then at United Airlines , Apple , and a downed internal communications network at the National Security Agency. There is no evidence that these systems disruptions affecting banking, airlines, tech giants, and the government are connected. items.title: Self-adjusting EEG helmet enables easy and reliable brainwave monitoring
items.summary: A self-adjusting electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring helmet has been developed to enable easier and more reliable brainwave measurements in various fields, including clinical settings, rehabilitation and brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). The helmet monitors electrode–scalp contact conditions in real time and automatically adjusts electrode positions to maintain stable contact. By reducing measurement variability caused by differences in users' head shapes and hair conditions, the technology is expected to improve the reliability of EEG measurements.

items.title: Dual-targeted CAR T-cell therapy shows promise in patients with treatment-resistant multiple myeloma
items.summary: A first-in-human study by Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute investigators found that a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy called TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. TriPRIL—short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation-inducing ligand)—recognizes two proteins on myeloma cells instead of just one. Researchers published their findings in The Lancet.

items.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
items.summary: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.

To get there, he applied to 15 colleges all over the U.S., narrowing it down to a final three. items.title: Trump to meet Putin in China amid renewed push to end Ukraine war
items.author: Barak Ravid
items.summary: President Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during the trilateral summit in China, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The meeting in Shenzhen will take place as Trump is making another push for a breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Also on Thursday, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet in Berlin with Ukrainian and European officials to work on security guarantees for Ukraine as well as a postwar Europe-Russia security architecture. They want to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi planned for next week. The big picture: The Trump-Putin meeting will take place on the sidelines of the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The summit wasn't intended to deal with Ukraine, but U.S. allies are bracing for Trump to make unexpected public statements that serve the interests of Russia and China. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.

items.title: Hikes to hikes? Parks in Minneapolis and suburbs look to fee increases to stay standing
items.author: Trevor Mitchell
items.summary: Amid a daunting budget season in Minneapolis and Hennepin County, the region’s widely-regarded park systems are looking to bolster their revenues by increasing fees on a number of services in the coming years — some for the first time ever. The increases will affect family essentials, like sports, summer camps and swimming pools, but officials say costs overall will remain affordable compared to private options and some nearby cities. And with the help of added revenue, the parks expect to stave off layoffs or reduced hours at rec centers. Three Rivers Park District Superintendent Boe Carlson presented his department’s proposed $57.4 million budget , which includes a 3.8% increase in its property tax levy, at a Hennepin County Board meeting on Nov. 17. Fees would go up by 3% for overnight camping, summer camps and merchandise sales, as well as cross-country skiing, tubing and the swim ponds. Carlson said the adjustments were “based on the inflationary increases we’re seeing around us,” but added that the district has a variety of fee assistance programs . items.title: New Oregon revenue forecast predicts $245M more than expected for next budget cycle
items.author: Dirk VanderHart
items.summary: With a looming Dec. 1 deadline to introduce her next two-year budget, Gov. Tina Kotek has a bit more money to spend. Oregon’s latest revenue forecast, delivered to lawmakers by state economists Wednesday, predicts the state can expect about $245 million more in the upcoming budget cycle than previously expected. It’s not an amount of money any Oregonian would scoff at, but in the context of the state budget, Chief Oregon Economist Carl Riccadonna cast the new forecast as something of a snooze. “The overarching theme of this forecast is: no news,” Riccadonna told reporters in a briefing Tuesday evening. What the economist meant, he said, is that the latest numbers largely bear out a prediction he delivered three months ago, when he told lawmakers Oregon’s economy appeared to be picking up steam. Riccadonna said healthy consumer spending and corporate profits continue to buoy the state and national economies. He acknowledged that Oregon had begun to once again lag behind the rest of the country when it comes to economic growth, but said he was “optimistic” that would be temporary. items.author: Matthew Martin
items.summary: The US and Iran traded fire over the last 24 hours, engulfing more of the Gulf states in their conflict, with Tehran launching strikes at US military targets in Bahrain and Kuwait, as well as UAE ships in the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington attacked missile launch sites on Qeshm Island. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said it continued to intercept missiles fired by Iranian-supported Houthi militias in Yemen, including at Riyadh. An uptick in attacks from both sides is indicative of a deepening stalemate , Reuters reported. Qatar’s foreign ministry called Iran’s actions — its strikes on Kuwait were its first in over two months — “ a dangerous escalation ” that would undermine ongoing diplomatic efforts to resolve the nine-month conflict. ADNOC Logistics & Services said one person was missing and 11 were injured after one of its vessels was hit while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. items.title: Madden review – Nicolas Cage is a cartoonish NFL legend in David O Russell’s stinker
items.author: Andrew Lawrence
items.summary: Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying. That the Madden video game franchise outlived the avuncular Minnesotan , whose death at age 85 in 2021 was mourned throughout the sport, is as much a testament to his singular knack for teaching the game’s fundaments as it is to his willingness to bring his classroom to students, wherever they might huddle. But Madden, a new Amazon biopic that can’t decide whether it’s serious or slapstick, has drawn all the wrong lessons.

items.title: Fermi’s 14-Year All-Sky Map Bridges Astronomy’s Elusive "MeV Gap"
items.author: Andy Tomaswick
items.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We’ve always had trouble measuring them in the “mega-electron volt” (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the “MeV gap”. But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. items.author: Nick Lichtenberg
items.summary: For most of this year, markets have been asking how big the AI bubble is and how bad it gets if it pops. On Wednesday, the European Central Bank went through the boom against the last big credit bust, point by point, using the companies’ own filings. In its twice-yearly Financial Stability Review , the ECB estimated that big tech firms had “total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than USD 4 trillion as of the second quarter of 2026,” which it said was “well in excess of their outstanding on-balance-sheet liabilities.” The sample is Alphabet , Amazon , Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Oracle , Broadcom and Anthropic. “The rapid shift towards debt finance invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles,” the central bank wrote. The ECB’s count lands a day after the Federal Reserve’s. In its own November Financial Stability Report, the Fed counted more than $3 trillion in signed leases that haven’t started yet, take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees at seven big tech companies, none of it showing up as debt, as Fortune reported . items.title: Jensen Huang and Nvidia is not a honeypot story. It is a national security story
items.author: Andrew King
items.summary: The consensus view: a brilliant engineer, seduced by a foreign agent. It is also Jensen Huang’s most convenient defense, turning a compliance failure into a private indiscretion. The narrative has one fatal flaw: Mr. Huang himself. A year ago, we brought the story to The Times of London , worked with the reporter based on our knowledge of the tactics, prompting the article, Beijing’s “sex warfare” in Silicon Valley in which we were quoted, and which Elon Musk summarized: “If she’s a 10, you’re an asset.” This is not a honeypot story, but it may be one of complicity. Megaspeed, a Singapore company, imported at least 136,000 Nvidia processors worth at least $4.6 billion, Bloomberg reports, more than half were Blackwell chips, restricted from sale to China. It bought through Aivres Systems, the California arm of Inspur, blacklisted for aiding China’s military. A Shanghai sister network, Century Litong facilitated up to $7.5 billion, The Information reports. The executive at the center of both, Alice Huang, is suspected of spying for China. items.title: Bouncing sand grains may explain planet-wide dust storms on Mars

items.title: 105 major housing markets to enter 2027 above this key inventory threshold
items.author: Lance Lambert
items.summary: Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter . During the Pandemic Housing Boom, housing demand was running so hot—and homes sold so quickly—listings barely even registered as active inventory. Indeed, in October 2021, there were only 565,707 active homes for sale, according to Realtor.com ’s data series. That was a staggering -53.8% below the 1,208,311 active listings in October 2019. At the end of October 2020 and October 2021, not a single one of America’s 200 largest metro area housing markets had more inventory than in pre-pandemic October 2019. Fast-forward to the end of October 2026, and there were 1,183,520 active homes for sale (just -2.1% below pre-pandemic 2019 levels)—and now 105 of the nation’s 200 largest housing markets have more active inventory than they did in pre-pandemic October 2019. items.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
items.author: Adrian Chiles
items.summary: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever. Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. I don’t know whether it’s because I’m drawn to the small phone screen, or rather that I find absorption with whatever I’m watching on the big flatscreen just too much to bear.

items.title: The hypothalamus is not a bystander in Alzheimer's disease
items.summary: Alzheimer's disease is well known as a disease of memory. But long before memory fades, many patients have trouble sleeping, lose their daily rhythms and show changes in metabolism and stress hormones. All of these functions are regulated by the hypothalamus, a structure at the base of the brain. A new study from the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, published on Nov. 18, 2026, in Nature, shows that the hypothalamus is not a bystander in Alzheimer's. Its circadian and metabolic control centers show specific age-related changes in volume and gene activity early in the disease.

items.summary: House Democrats voted at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday morning to nominate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as their candidate for speaker. Why it matters: It's a symbolic but significant step that suggests Jeffries has the votes he needs to be elected the first Black House speaker on Jan. 3. Jeffries won 251 of the 262 votes cast, putting him comfortably above the 218 votes he needs to win on the House floor in January. The vote was tallied at Jeffries' request . His allied had initially hoped he would be elected by acclamation, but the Democratic leader changed tack at the 11th hour and decided to call his detractors' bluff. Between the lines: Wednesday's caucus vote was a secret ballot. On Jan. 3, each House member will have to stand up during a televised proceeding and announce who they are voting for. That could be difficult for the members — particularly progressives — who have been flooded with calls and emails from constituents urging them not to vote for him. Only a handful of incoming House members, including Reps.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) and Don Leonard (D-Ohio), have outright said they will oppose Jeffries thus far.

items.author: Armend Nimani / AFP / Getty
items.summary: O n the eighth day of violent protests in Tirana, I followed a column of some 3,000 people marching through the Albanian capital. For months, Albanians had held anti-government demonstrations as peaceful as the pink bird that had lent their movement its name—the Flamingo Revolution. But the protests had recently entered a new, volatile phase. Some had begun calling it the Eagle Revolution, after the fiercer bird on the national flag. It was 1 p.m. on a Tuesday in October, and demonstrators filled the downtown boulevards. We walked past shattered bus shelters, broken shop windows, and government buildings blackened by fire. “Down with the patronazhistët ,” people shouted, referring to the entrenched patronage networks that reward party loyalty over merit in nearly every sphere of life. When another group chanted a World War II slogan—“Albania for the Albanians, death to the traitors”—my fixer said, “This one is for you.” He meant Americans. What had first sparked the protests, in May, were plans by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of the American president, to build an ultra-luxury resort in a fragile nature preserve in the country’s south, where flamingos gather. items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.author: Emma Brockes
items.summary: He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us. And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof. items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.author: Emma Russell
items.summary: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.

items.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
items.author: Interview by Imogen Tilden
items.summary: Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different. Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.

items.summary: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson . While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago. Here is what a decade without a hospital labor and delivery unit looks like: Pregnant patients with insurance are told to find care in another county. After they finished they raced onto the next field, jostling each other, leaping over a herding dog and chomping the overgrown vegetation. As the animals crowded into the untreated field, mother does guided their kids to patches of grass, and larger animals stood up against an oak tree to browse the leaves. items.title: We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it
items.author: Roee Naim
items.summary: I run Tutorela , a U.S. tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions. I’m saying that up front because this piece argues for that model, and because we learned the lesson behind it the hard way. Alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina. As districts decide how much of the school day to hand to software, they should hear what happened when we gave students the best learning tool we could build. We built it. They didn’t come. For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons. To fill the gap between those lessons, we built a math learning and practice app with more than 10,000 exercises. Every problem came with a full solution in text and video, and we made the whole thing a game, with progress and rewards, so practice would feel less like homework. A year ago we added an AI assistant that could walk a student through any step, any time, for free. By any product standard it was the best a student could get. items.summary: McGill University researchers have developed and tested a new way to facilitate the creation of personalized genetic therapies for children with rare neurodevelopmental disorders. Currently, many children suffering from rare disorders are left without a realistic path to treatment, given that the underlying genetic changes may affect only a handful of patients. items.title: How to Fix the Country

items.summary: When the 39th Congress convened on December 4, 1865, it was the first time the nation’s representatives had gathered since the Confederacy’s defeat and the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln. In the nine months Congress had been in recess, the Southern states had reconstituted their governments under the auspices of President Andrew Johnson, a Southerner whose commitment to the union was giving way to his virulent racism. From the sidelines, Lincoln’s fellow Republicans watched in horror as Southerners re-erected slavery’s scaffolding by restricting the freed population’s rights and condemning them to field labor. South Carolina and Mississippi elected Confederate generals as their governors. In Louisiana, former Confederate officers conducted state business in rebel uniforms. So when Congress came together, the Republican majority had to decide how to move the nation forward. Would they let the South return to its old ways over the bodies of more than 600,000 soldiers, or would they seize the chance to shape a society of equals? items.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.summary: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

items.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

This could make it difficult for African-owned development banks to secure higher ratings without bringing in non-African shareholders, effectively forcing these lenders to surrender part of their ownership and control. In the case of assessments of multilateral banks, rating methodologies have a bias towards non-African shareholders. items.title: SpaceX $40 billion chip financing to stay off balance sheet
items.author: Ellen DiMauro
items.summary: The colossal $40 billion financing that Apollo is lining up for SpaceX could hit markets as early as this week, but it won’t be hitting their balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter. The financing will go into an SPV, or special-purpose vehicle, allowing SpaceX to keep it off its own balance sheet and instead rent GPUs from its subsidiary. Apollo will be lending close to $20 billion of the deal upfront and then syndicating it or selling it to other investors later. Other companies, including Meta, have utilized this kind of financial workarounds to keep debt off their bottom lines. It also allows the companies to keep their ratings elevated. Portions of the seven-part deal could be sold to investors as early as this week. The arrangement includes an array of pricing — the bulk of which, $35.5 billion, will price at 8.3% and 7.75%, Semafor reported earlier . Other, riskier parts of the deal will price even higher, at a blended rate that could exceed 9%, but will account for less than $3 billion of the overall financing. items.summary: Maybe you remember them: the credit-card offers—so congratulatory, so seductive—that pour into graduating college seniors’ mailboxes. To the unwary, they seem to promise free money. In practice, they can often lead to debt. This is what happens to Becky Bloomwood, the protagonist of the chick-lit classic Confessions of a Shopaholic , by the British writer Sophie Kinsella. The novel opens with a bank offering Becky an extended overdraft of £2,000 for her first two years in the workforce. Mere pages later, the two years are up, and Becky, now a financial journalist with a serious shopping habit, owes the bank thousands of pounds. Confessions of a Shopaholic came out in the United States 25 years ago, and certain aspects of the book haven’t aged at all: Becky’s chatty warmth is as enjoyable as ever, and the debt she racks up will likely be relatable to as many readers now as in the early aughts. But the details and texture of her shopping—physical credit cards swiped, department stores wandered through—are so unlike the reality of today’s consumerism, with its smartphones and scrolling, that the novel is almost a time capsule. About three dozen cows bound down the hill to gobble up the morning snack — a byproduct of the organic grains Hafner has grown on this farm for decades. “It’s like candy to a cow,” he said. “I mean, they love it.” His son Jeff Hafner now owns the farm and manages the day-to-day operations. But Earl still helps out. Jeff jokes that his father retired to an 8-hour day. “I don’t sleep well unless I work hard during the day,” Earl said. Although he’s still up early to feed cattle and will get in the combine to harvest fields after that, Earl has gradually stepped back from managing the farm, allowing Jeff to take the lead. That change took years, and Earl much prefers it to the alternative. Earl Hafner shows the milled wheat chaff, or mids, he feeds to the cattle. The two are expected to hold a summit Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the three are expected to talk about nuclear arms control, Iran, Ukraine, trade and AI chips. Driving the news: Trump arrived in China for the annual APEC conference just hours after spending time in the Philippines. Xi met Trump at the bottom of Air Force One's stairs. The two leaders shook hands and then embraced in a hug. Dozens of performers, waving pom-poms, stood on a red carpet outside the plane, chanting and cheering for Trump's arrival. Context: Xi's surprise appearance was an unusual diplomatic gesture, per multiple reports . The Chinese president did not personally greet Trump when he visited Beijing in May. items.title: The DRC's Ebola outbreak remains out of control
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak is spiralling , with the disease spreading at a record pace despite a surge in funding. Rampant misinformation, widespread violence, and a lack of medical equipment have aided the spread of the Bundibugyo strain, which is now Africa’s biggest-ever Ebola outbreak by geographic reach. A lack of treatments or vaccines has also meant that the current outbreak is more fatal than ever: Around 50% of those who are infected die, the highest-ever mortality rate for Ebola. Although authorities are seeking more funding, more than $700 million remains unaccounted for by the DRC, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, while frontline workers have gone unpaid for months. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: US technology outages spark paranoia
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: Technology outages in the US disrupted everything from air travel to secretive government work, fueling public distrust and paranoia. Purchases of non-perishable goods, batteries, and generators are soaring , leading some analysts to raise the share price forecast for wholesaler Costco. Though it is highly unusual for so many outages to occur in such a brief period of time, experts have largely discarded the possibility of attacks, arguing the disruptions were more likely caused by outdated software and equipment. The world probably faces a “period of transition” in which hackers will hold the upper hand over defenders, AI expert Yann LeCun said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, though he noted future software would be “hardened” by AI. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

The transformation is notable: When Washington shepherded Beijing into the World Trade Organization 25 years ago, “the US thought it could change China,” Bloomberg noted. “ Instead, China changed the US .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? items.author: Catherina Gioino
items.summary: American workers have spent three years too stuck to quit . But in 2027, Indeed and Glassdoor say that’s when it ends, one way or another. Quits are running about 349,000 a month below what current worker unhappiness would predict, according to Indeed and Glassdoor’s 2027 U.S. Hiring and Worklife Trends Report. The share of Glassdoor reviewers rating their career opportunities one or two stars hit 21% in September, up from 17% in April 2022. And over the same stretch, the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ quits rate fell from 3.3% to 2.1%. The report says that pressure will break in 2027, either through a hiring rebound that sets off a wave of quitting, or through a downturn that brings layoffs. Laura Ullrich, director of economic research at Indeed and a former Richmond Fed economist , said that the second path can arrive without warning. “Economic expansions don’t die of old age; they’re murdered,” she said, recalling a line economists used at the central bank. “You find out overnight, like something’s happened,” Ullrich said. “So that could happen in 2027. She can picture a better experience. In the past, getting there meant comparing a dozen visitor-management vendors, picking the closest fit, and bending her process to what the software could do. The system she created from scratch checks guests in, alerts their hosts in Slack, handles signed NDAs, and syncs with the calendar for expected visitors. items.title: The outages America has suffered weren't an attack, but the next failure could be
items.summary: The recent string of outages is a statistical cluster that exposes real fragility, not coordinated sabotage — but it should still wake us up. Over the past week, Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, went dark worldwide after a latent defect from a July network update surfaced under heavy load. Next, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop after routers at sites in Arkansas and Texas overwhelmed aging air traffic control systems. Then Chase and other banks saw transaction slowdowns from a software bug. United delayed departures because of an internal system failure. And finally, reports emerged of disruptions to the NSA’s classified internal network. Officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have stated they are highly confident these were unrelated technical issues, not a cyberattack. But we humans are wired to seek patterns. Events this close together feel ominous. In this case, the evidence points to a predictable downside of efficiency: concentrated cloud computing dependencies and incompletely tested updates that create single points of failure across email, aviation, finance and more. The company built its own dataset of over 10 million labels, using teams of trained sniffers and spectrometers running around the clock. Real-world applications — and real skeptics: Osmo has worked with P&G on fragrances, identified insect repellents stronger than DEET, and helped spot counterfeit sneakers. items.title: A New Milestone for Life on Earth
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic *
items.summary: For 4.5 billion years, Earth’s relationship with the cosmos involved only stuff falling onto our planet from space. Back when Earth was just a small pile of rocks, it grew thanks to torrents of additional rocks raining down upon it. Later, the water of our oceans was likely delivered by comets and asteroids, which also dispensed starter packs of organic molecules that may have been essential to getting life going. And then, just recently, Earth reversed the flow. About 70 years ago, humans packed small boxes of electronics—the first satellites—into rockets and blasted them into orbit. Now we’ve stuffed Earth’s orbit to the gills and visited every planet in the solar system with our robot emissaries. We’ve even sent out probes that will one day travel beyond the sun’s reach. This morning, around a quarter past 5, one of those probes crossed a milestone at that frontier, passing one light-day of distance from its home world. Voyager 1 had already traveled farther from Earth than had any other human artifact. items.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
items.author: Michael Donkor
items.summary: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

items.title: In Utah, a ‘hydrocarbon highway’ could run right through this petroglyph-filled canyon

Earlier this year, the Trump administration approved plans to blast a “ hydrocarbon highway ” connecting nearby oil fields to rail-loading facilities through Nine Mile Canyon’s cultural and archaeological-rich sites. Last month environmental and historic preservation groups sued to stop them. “It’s like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum,” said J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, in a statement. The Trump administration resurrected the project in eastern Utah after it stalled out during President Joe Biden’s term. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit say approvals for the highway bypassed the normal public comment and ecological review processes. The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and the Center for Biological Diversity filed their complaint in Utah’s U.S. District Court against the Department of Interior and Bureau of Land Management. items.title: What Congress’ bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you
items.author: Austin Corona
items.summary: The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in Arizona and California, faced opposition from birders, the military, and tribes. While some disputes were resolved, tribes’ concerns about the project’s impacts on historic sites have remained unsettled, leading to court battles that still haven’t been resolved even though the line was completed in June. Such legal challenges commonly delay renewable energy projects and the transmission lines that carry their power to population centers. The threat of lawsuits and resistance from utilities have driven down long-distance power line construction in the United States, limiting the country’s ability to use cheap renewable energy. The Senate is poised to pass a “permitting reform” bill that could make it much faster and easier to build transmission lines and renewable energy projects — but it casts a wide net, easing construction for almost all large infrastructure projects. items.title: They migrated to New York for work. Now they’re fighting to climate-proof it.
items.author: Frida Garza
items.summary: Earlier this year, riding his e-bike through New York City’s bustling streets on a sweltering July afternoon, José Yos began to smell smoke. It wasn’t coming from a nearby burning building or a beat-up yellow cab. Instead, the smell came from hundreds of miles away in Canada. Raging wildfires in Quebec had sent a cloud of thick, smoky air toward the city, blanketing it in a strange orange haze. It wasn’t the first time Yos, a 40-year-old from Guatemala who delivers food and groceries on apps like DoorDash, had experienced this. In 2023, Canada had its worst wildfire season on record, with around 37 million acres (15 million hectares) of land going up in flames. Wildfire smoke traveled down from Quebec to New York , polluting the air and turning the skies a deep shade of orange . This summer, though, the city was also in the middle of a heat emergency — its second in as many weeks. The temperature was projected to reach close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit that day, and the heat index — the day’s real feel temperature — was supposed to be even higher. items.title: Meet the Teen Who Called a Hospital Home
items.author: Cara Anthony
items.summary: ST. LOUIS — The teen’s hospital stay began in room 3005. The room didn’t feel like home at first. Back then, Jaloni didn’t have posters on the wall or snacks on the shelf, and he hadn’t learned about the morgue yet. He just wanted to survive. Fresh gunshot wounds filled the 14-year-old’s body with unbearable pain. That first night, Jaloni said, he could barely move. But in his own way, Jaloni could fly. His pain medication was so strong that the teenager said he felt like he was soaring in a dream. In reality, though, Jaloni was a teenager caught between two worlds. Around his friends he had been a fearless risk-taker who knew how to steal without getting caught. Inside the hospital, Jaloni was now a boy who needed his grandmother to tell him that everything would be OK and that somehow life would get better as soon as he was released from the hospital. But she couldn’t make that promise. No one could. He ended up staying in the SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital for more than 475 days over the next three years, his medical records show. In the complaint, Young, a Black woman, alleges she was discriminated against by the county in a series of incidents between January 2025 and June 2026, which amounted to her being paid substantially less than her white counterparts and targeted with stricter work requirements after raising the payment concerns with county officials. A recent report by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to Congress stated that the cost of consumer fraud targeting older adults (60 and older) could have been as high as $119.5 billion last year. Plus, the risk of higher median losses also occurred with older adults, with a large disparity for those 80 years old and older. When it comes to preying on older adults, scammers come from far and wide. items.title: The FBI is changing how it fights crime and protects Americans in their communities
items.summary: When President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, America faced one of the highest threat environments in its history. Years of open borders, soft-on-crime policies and a government that turned its back on law enforcement had left our communities vulnerable and our law enforcement officers without the support they deserved. Under Trump’s leadership, we set out to reverse that tide. We rebuilt the FBI around its core mission: protecting the American people. We changed our priorities, revitalized partnerships, overhauled our technology and transformed the Bureau into a more aggressive, effective crime-fighting organization. The results: Over the last 21 months, this FBI made 71,650 violent crime arrests , a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration. We seized 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans. items.title: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. Coates was only eight years old at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. items.summary: When DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart for $17 billion, the deal yoked rival food delivery companies that already shared a common link: the same venture firm lurking in both boardrooms. Alfred Lin, a partner at Sequoia Capital, sits on DoorDash’s board while Ravi Gupta, also a Sequoia partner, is Instacart’s lead independent director. That kind of arrangement, in which partners from the same investment firm sit on the boards of competing companies, is exactly what the Department of Justice is reportedly probing at venture capital Andreessen Horowitz . And for some antitrust scholars, the DoorDash-Instacart cash and stock deal is exactly why that kind of investor interlock matters. A danger of interlocking directors is that companies become less likely to compete, said Mark Lemley, the William H. Neukom Professor at Stanford Law School, “because the directors have fiduciary duties to both companies, so they don’t want to encourage one company to do anything that would hurt the other.” Another danger? items.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
items.author: Michael Segalov
items.summary: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash.

items.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
items.author: Luca Turin
items.summary: Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. items.title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.summary: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. items.summary: As AI-enabled drones transform the way wars are fought in Ukraine and Iran, two leaders of military tech startups warned on Tuesday that the Pentagon has to move faster to keep up with modern warfare. “There’s a growing realization that if you don’t act now, it will be existential in the near future,” Tyler Sweatt, CEO of defense software deployment company Second Front Systems, told Fortune ’s Allie Garfinkle at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum . He said it was the largest and most important church in medieval Makuria, one of three kingdoms that emerged along the middle reaches of the Nile River following the arrival of Christian missionaries in the sixth century. In addition to the Original Recipe Chicken and Zinger, our menu offers energy bowls and sparkling coffee – many of which cannot be found in KFC menus outside China. More broadly, we have adapted everything from marketing to store formats as consumer preferences, technology and competition have evolved. For any global brand, keeping pace with such change requires tremendous effort. I believe one reason KFC has been able to keep adapting is the strength of our local teams. They have the know-how and autonomy to respond to the market with agility. The brand may be global, but decisions are made close to the consumer. KFC is one of the six restaurant brands operated by Yum China , which together span 20,000 stores across the country. The injunction will prevent uncertainty about the scope of court orders that found a similar 2023 law unconstitutional and “avert inconsistent enforcement of a statute that plaintiffs have shown is likely unconstitutional,” Halligan wrote. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012. One was a 14-year-old girl who had called more than 100 people trying to get mental health care before she ended up in his hospital with broken legs. Another was a 21-year-old with meningitis. “She wakes up. What’s the first thing she says? I’m a single mother. I can’t afford this. I got to get out of here,” Conway said. The third was a 15-year-old on Medicaid who needed complex rehab for a neurologic disorder, and the hospital was struggling to find anywhere to send her. “That should not happen in America, but it does every single day,” he said. During the week, Conway runs Optum, the health services arm of UnitedHealth Group, which he said employs about 300,000 of the conglomerate’s roughly 400,000 people. That makes him one of the more unusual witnesses to American health care’s failures, because his company sits on the other side of many of them. The discovery is described in a paper published in the journal Zootaxa by scientists from Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense in Indonesia, the University of California, Davis, and other collaborators.

items.title: Turning food waste into insect feed poses only low mad cow disease risk
items.summary: Insects can convert food waste and by-products from the food industry (such as unsold ready meals or slaughter by-products) into ingredients for animal feed. In this way, they can contribute to the transition toward a circular food production system, in which what would otherwise be wasted is reused. However, these waste streams may contain animal proteins that pose a risk of transmitting diseases such as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), also known as mad cow disease. For this reason, rearing insects on waste streams containing animal proteins is not permitted in the European Union.

items.title: The Gulf's oil-eating microbes lay in wait before Deepwater Horizon spill, frozen samples suggest
items.author: Clay Wear
items.summary: A year before the Deepwater Horizon spill, a NOAA crew scooped up seawater from the Gulf and froze it. items.title: Lasers near physical limits of miniaturization open possibilities for tracking life at the nanoscale
items.summary: From tracking how cancer develops to exploring how the brain works, scientists need ways to observe biological processes at increasingly smaller scales. Beyond tracking how cells move and interact, researchers need to understand how tiny structures within cells, including organelles and molecular complexes, behave and change over time. However, identifying and tracking these microscopic targets individually remains a major challenge.

items.title: Optimized supercomputer workflow accelerates protein-structure prediction
items.summary: A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)-led team has harnessed the power of El Capitan to accelerate generation of predicted protein structures, drastically reducing the computing time required and opening new possibilities for drug discovery, biological research and national security applications.

items.title: New model identifies priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile
items.summary: Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

items.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
items.author: Nathan Bomey
items.summary: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday. The popular Gen-Z-targeted account is characterized by its quick-turn analysis on progressive, left-wing topics ranging from identity politics to mental health and niche internet trends. That winning formula caught the attention of social video publisher NowThis , which recently acquired the brand. Launched in 2020 by founders Tim Chau and Michelle Andrews, the Impact Instagram handle was born in the apex of Gen Z’s formative years, an era marked by a hyper-online generation who reckoned with Donald Trump, COVID-19, social isolation, canceled graduations, the murder of George Floyd, and climate disaster all in the same year. Impact created timely stories around narratives that Gen Z desperately craved and traditional media often failed to cover: Its content is often among the first to share pointed commentary on trending headlines. items.title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
items.summary: At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths. The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army , the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant. Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action. The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, of Celina, Texas. items.title: An Obituary for America’s Measles-Elimination Status
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic
items.summary: UNITED STATES—A scientific triumph that quietly shaped a generation, the United States’ measles-elimination status passed away on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Hailed as an unmitigated good and a borderline miracle on its initial appearance, then quickly forgotten, Measles Elimination had seemed to have many more good years ahead of it. Its decline was sudden and dramatic, and it had been feuding with the secretary of health and human services for some time, although he denied having any direct role in its demise. Observers described its death as “senseless,” “utterly senseless,” “an enormous step backward,” and “the kind of thing that makes you lose all hope in human progress.” Measles Elimination arrived in 2000 as the proud work of scientists and doctors and public messaging. Praised at the time as one of the country’s greatest public-health achievements, it had hoped to make way for many more such eliminations. “Now, instead, we are looking at the first of many obituaries that didn’t need to be written,” one observer commented. The 49-year-old spacecraft will reach a point about 16 billion miles from Earth — the distance that light travels in 24 hours. Scientists call that unit a light-day. And while it’s not a particularly meaningful scientific measurement, it’s a pretty good opportunity to marvel at how far Voyager has voyaged. The craft first set out in 1977 to explore our solar system’s outer planets, including Jupiter and Saturn. It flew past both planets, snapping photos of their surfaces and making several big discoveries , before reaching interstellar space in 2012. Today, both Voyager and its sister, Voyager 2, remain part of an active NASA mission measuring the gases and magnetic field outside the Sun’s protective magnetic bubble. items.title: BREAKING: Everything
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.summary: A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay , a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging. Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight. Read full article Comments

items.title: Bry Reed: Remembering Saint Bea
items.author: Bry Reed
items.summary: I’m worried about surviving the winter. I’ve been thinking about the cold months of the year since summer. In part my worry is about what it’ll cost me (financially and emotionally) to survive early sunsets, chilling winds, and whatever precipitation falls. Groceries, heat, warm clothing, vitamins, medicine, and everything else that makes winter bearable is costing more and more money. I’m worried about how federal budget cuts and the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 (known as the Farm Bill) will impact me and my neighbors. The legislation, which has passed the House, is due to be voted on by the Senate in the coming weeks. Its content touches everything from agriculture and food to nature conservation, energy, forestry, and environmental law and could be the law of the land until 2031 if passed. Legislation like the Farm Bill is a piece of my worry, but not all of it. My primary concern is how folks will meet their immediate needs. How many people are choosing between heat and groceries with BGE rate hikes looming? My worries mount and I search through my childhood for memories of how my family prepared for winters in the early 2000s. How did we survive then, and how

items.title: Jerrell Gibbs brings viewers home to his multisensory memories of Baltimore in BMA show
items.author: Rhea Ramakrishnan
items.summary: At the opening of “Jerrell Gibbs: Come home with me” in September at the Baltimore Museum of Art, a member of the museum’s staff remarked that the paint had just finished drying. I thought it was a figure of speech, but they may have meant it literally. All 32 of the paintings featured in the exhibit were painted between February and September of this year. But the work isn’t about newness; it is inspired by the house of Gibbs’ Aunt Ella, where he grew up. Each wing of the exhibit is dedicated to a specific location in the home. We start on the porch and then migrate into the living room, the kitchen, the backyard, and the basement. It all has the warmth of a place that’s been lived in — the kind of family home you can drop by on a whim, and though your hosts keep apologizing for the mess, everything always looks quite artfully arranged and, more importantly, welcoming. Gibbs grew up in the Woodmere neighborhood of Park Heights in Northwest Baltimore, and he can describe both his home and his childhood vividly. Aunt Ella’s house was a colonial rowhome, and its architecture will be familiar to most people from Baltimore. What was unique about this particular rowhome, though, was tha

items.title: Mourning a lost legend
items.author: Eze Jackson
items.summary: John Dierker, legendary local saxophone and clarinet player, was murdered while riding his bike at Leakin Park on November 10. More than just a world class musician and Towson University music professor, Dierker was a crucial part of many Baltimore music scenes. Tributes to him by fellow musicians have poured out over the last week and will continue for a long time to come. Dierker’s impact on music in Baltimore expands far beyond his own name. He played with the New Volcanoes and Microkingdom. He collaborated with Will Redman in 2020 on “Ten Thousand Percent,” and with Jeff Arnal on the 2023 EP “Astral Chronology.” Most recently, in March of this year he joined longtime comrades Jarrett Gilgore, Mike Kuhl, and Chris Pumphrey on “Empty Into Fullness.” It’s a 24-minute and 56-second track that came out of an experience of being at a performance where the room felt heavy. The quartet channeled that experience into an instrumental journey of meditative emotional processing in the way artists so often are able to find solace using the tools they have. You could find John at Baltimore Boom Bap Society contributing to improvised hip-hop, or jamming with a jazz band at Joe Squared. The be

The project has centered on 14 speculative works commissioned by the project to reimagine “Baltimore’s founding river,” along with historical documents and images pertaining to it. items.title: SBA chief defends policy barring green-card holders from loans, even if they can serve in U.S. military
items.author: Tatiana Sataua
items.summary: Small Business Administration chief Kelly Loeffler said Tuesday it’s “completely not true” that her agency’s new loan rules restrict immigrants. The rules she was defending bar green-card holders, who can legally work, pay taxes and, if otherwise eligible, enlist in the U.S. military, from SBA-backed loans. Under a policy that took effect March 1 , businesses must be wholly owned by U.S. citizens or nationals to qualify for SBA-backed loans, cutting out lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green-card holders, who were previously eligible. In fiscal 2025, the agency approved 3,358 loans to businesses partly owned by lawful permanent residents, about 4% of its 85,000 loan approvals, according to the SBA . This puzzling inconsistency is one of the main reasons immunotherapies don't work in most cancer patients.

items.title: Mississippi holds nation’s highest preterm birth rate, report shows
items.author: Sophia Paffenroth
items.summary: Preterm birth is more common in Mississippi than anywhere else in the country, leading the state to receive a failing grade in the March of Dimes’ 2026 annual report card for the 19th year in a row. In 2025, 14.9% of Mississippi babies were born before 37 weeks gestation – down slightly from 15% in 2024. The report card from the March of Dimes, a national nonprofit organization aimed at improving the health of caregivers and babies, said this is not a statistically significant improvement. In fact, Mississippi only saw a statistically significant change in its preterm birth rate over the last decade in 2016, 2018 and 2021 – all years when the rate increased. Black babies were more likely than white babies to be born prematurely, at 18.8% and 12.7% respectively. Last year, 4,894 babies in the state were born preterm, which the report attributes mainly to policy decisions and chronic diseases. Policy decisions include the state’s failure to expand Medicaid, adopt paid parental leave policies and implement Medicaid reimbursement for doulas. The Board of Trustees didn’t take an up-or-down vote on the raise itself at its meeting Monday night, but instead referred the question of whether to amend Garcia’s current contract to the Board Operations Committee, which Chair Janna Hafer said would likely meet Thursday. Board Operations is where negotiations for the superintendent’s contract are supposed to take place, under district policy. But in this case, those talks began at a special board meeting, called in response to information that Garcia was interviewing for another superintendent job elsewhere. Garcia declined to confirm any details about that interview in a Tuesday text message with Montana Free Press. Hafer told MTFP Monday night that she called the special meeting to ensure all board members could weigh in, and that she alone wouldn’t decide whether to open the door to mid-year contract talks aimed at keeping Garcia on board. items.summary: Several years ago, a researcher from Kyoto University was conducting fieldwork in Borneo in an effort to understand why certain primates frequently choose trees along rivers as sleeping sites. Among other potential hypotheses, he wondered whether there were fewer mosquitoes along riverbanks, allowing primates to sleep more comfortably. This question soon motivated him and his team of researchers to investigate how mosquito abundance varies between riverbanks and inland forests.

items.title: Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars
items.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. Now, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has analyzed over a decade of this data to determine whether the daily and seasonal changes in Mars' atmosphere could be explained by known processes, including the freezing and release of carbon dioxide at its poles. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface.

items.title: New nanoparticle MRI probe enables quantitative pH imaging
items.summary: The acidity of tissues can provide important clues about a disease. Tumors and inflamed tissues often become more acidic than their surroundings because of changes in cellular metabolism. Measuring these pH variations could help researchers understand disease progression, identify abnormal tissue environments and evaluate treatment responses. However, detecting small pH differences inside the body remains challenging because magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals are affected by the concentration of the imaging agent used.

Unlike the familiar four-coordinate carbon in methane, the central carbon in these clusters can be coordinated by five or even six gold atoms.

items.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems

items.summary: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. In California, where Republicans lost every major race by landslides, voters rejected a billionaire wealth tax, made it harder to create one, and likely killed a measure that would have piloted public financing of elections. In Colorado, a deep blue electorate voted to ban gender surgeries on minors by 4 points and to bar trans athletes’ participation in female sports by 5 points. A similar sports proposal prevailed by 12 points in Washington, even as Democrats padded their state legislative majorities. And in Iowa, where Gov.-elect Rob Sand led a Democratic comeback, voters endorsed a two-thirds legislative supermajority for any income tax increase. The success of some conservative ideas down the ballot — largely focused on taxes and social issues — gave some hope to Republicans after a hopeless election night. items.summary: In 1962, my father faced a novel threat to the Constitution. The governor of Mississippi had defied a federal court order and physically blocked a young Black Air Force veteran from attending the University of Mississippi. As U.S. attorney general, my father—Robert F. Kennedy—knew he had to do something. The governor was backed by a state police force that acted as his personal militia. There was, and is, no federal police force that my father or his brother, President John F. Kennedy, could deploy to deal with a lawless chief executive at the state level. My father cobbled together a force of duly deputized U.S. marshals, many of them drawn from the ranks of the U.S. Border Patrol. He sent two courageous Justice Department attorneys—World War II veterans—to prepare the marshals before deploying them to Oxford, Mississippi. They were able, barely, to protect James Meredith on his first day at the university. Eventually, about 30,000 troops and National Guardsmen were activated to protect Meredith. The key idea being that, historically, illiberal powers in every era find each other and eventually conspire against the liberal world. In its specifics, Bush’s Axis of Evil didn’t make a ton of sense. Iran and Iraq were mortal enemies, not confederates. The North Koreans were happy to help anyone—Iran, Iraq, Pakistan—who paid.
