items.title: Joy, hope and anger as Serbia student movement’s political novices enter parliament
items.author: Guy de Launey in Belgrade
items.summary: Celebrating supporters say they feel vindicated by arrival of Student List candidates in national assembly The paved plateau in front of Serbia’s national assembly became an impromptu dancefloor, as people of all ages joyfully whirled in a kolo. Drivers passing by sounded their horns, while hundreds of people waved flags, blew whistles and cheered. Every now and again, the crowd parted, allowing smartly dressed men and women to walk up the steps and into the building. These were the candidates from the Student List, on their way to being sworn in as members of parliament after their stunning victory in last month’s parliamentary elections . Those who had come to cheer them on displayed their feelings on badges, flags and placards.

items.title: New World screwworm spreading rapidly across Southwestern states
items.author: Kevin Hardy for Stateline
items.summary: A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest. Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three states. While fewer than 10 total cases were recorded in August and September, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has already confirmed 53 cases this month. “We got a bunch more cases all of a sudden,” said David Anderson, professor and extension economist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University. Rising infections have pushed state leaders to designate certain outbreak areas across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, where animal movement is being restricted. The movement of pets and livestock is restricted in all or parts of 31 Texas counties as officials there are tracking 77 sites with at least one confirmed case. Contrary to its name, the screwworm grows into an adult fly about the size of a common housefly. items.title: The internet was built for Netflix streaming down to your couch. AT&T’s COO says AI agents are flipping it the other way
items.author: Nick Lichtenberg
items.summary: For two decades, the internet has mostly run one way: down. Netflix , YouTube and everything else stream from a data center to a couch, and the networks were built to match. AT&T’s chief operating officer says AI is starting to change that. “The actual direction of the bandwidth of the internet is undergoing a fundamental shift,” Jeff McElfresh said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. With agentic AI, he said, “we’re seeing agents tap the network in a 24 by seven, a very different approach. It’s not so episodic anymore.” U.S. household upload traffic grew 19.2% year-over-year in the second quarter, more than three times as fast as downloads, which grew 6.1%, according to OpenVault , which tracks broadband usage for internet providers. The average subscriber now uploads 58.2 GB a month. Households still download about 11x as much as they upload, but that ratio was 16.6x in 2019. For the companies spending hundreds of billions on AI and the networks that carry it, that matters: a lot of last-mile infrastructure was built on the assumption that people mostly watch, not send. ‘There’s the Netflix traffic’ McElfresh has been at AT&T for 31 years. items.author: Wen Shao
items.summary: Cognition’s AI coder just got promoted. The startup, currently valued at $48 billion, helped kick off the race to build coding agents with its viral product Devin. Now it is trying to get back to the front of the pack by debuting Devin Bots, a persistent coding tool that acts as a manager for teams of Devin agents that can manage a complex project over days or even weeks. In the past few months, several AI companies have rolled out always-on agents that are designed to be general-purpose, but can be used for coding tasks. OpenAI has unveiled Dots, an always-on proactive agent that integrates with its Codex product to run teams of agents handling software development tasks. Anthropic has unveiled a similar product called Duet that can integrate with its Claude Code product. But Cognition’s Devin Bots are some of the first to be designed specifically for software development. Texas went on to award Elon Musk’s SpaceX about $109 million to connect nearly 64,000 locations with Starlink, more than any other provider in the state. That reversal is now under scrutiny from state senators of both parties, the State Auditor, and the Democrats who take over the governor’s office and the attorney general’s office in January. Payments to every Texas grant recipient have been frozen since August. How fiber lost out to satellite Congress created the $42.5 billion Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program in 2021 as part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. BEAD was meant to bring high-speed internet to underserved areas, especially rural communities. The program got off to a slow start, and no new projects had broken ground by the end of 2024. items.title: Brain connectivity in high-traffic regions may shape how multiple sclerosis damages tissue
items.summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system mistakenly turns against the body's own cells. In this case, immune cells attack myelin, a fatty, protein-rich substance that forms a protective coating around nerve fibers. Myelin gives the brain's white matter its characteristic whitish appearance and helps nerve cells communicate with one another. However, the damage does not stop there. MS is also linked to the gradual shrinking or atrophy of gray matter, the brain tissue where most nerve cell bodies are found. As this tissue shrinks, people tend to experience more severe symptoms, including difficulties with movement and thinking.

items.title: Study finds that feeling ownership of a pain-relief object may help increase pain tolerance
items.summary: Pain relief may come from more than medication. A study by the Department of Psychology at Lingnan University has found that simply feeling a sense of ownership over an object believed to relieve pain may help people cope better with pain, even when the object itself contains no active ingredients. These findings have been published in The Journal of Pain and provide a new direction for exploring a low-cost approach to supporting pain management in health care.

items.title: Why punishment doesn't always prevent crime
items.summary: From "three-strikes" laws to longer prison sentences, harsher penalties are imposed in the hope they'll reduce crime. But decades of research show that increasing punishment often does surprisingly little. What if we're missing something crucial? New research from the University of California San Diego suggests one potentially overlooked reason: people's moral motivations for breaking the law in the first place.

items.title: This supernova is 50 million light-years away, but that's close enough for astronomers
items.summary: A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light-years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. It's not a core-collapse supernova, in which a massive star burns through its fuel, collapses and explodes. It's a Type Ia supernova. That means it's happening in a binary star system, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.

items.title: Women made history at the polls, but the fight for equality isn’t over
items.author: Alis Headlam
items.summary: This commentary is by Alis Headlam, a retired educator who writes commentaries on issues related to civil rights, education and faith. I was deeply touched by the song “ This Is Our Day ” by the Lyrical Lanterns, released ahead of International Women’s Day on March 8, 2026. It highlights the challenges women have faced while offering hope and encouragement: “Every scar became a story.” Those words capture something important about the history of women’s progress: Every struggle has helped open doors for those who follow. We have come so far. The history of women’s rights in the United States reflects a long and often difficult struggle for equality and justice. In 1848, the Seneca Falls Convention, organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and other reformers, produced the Declaration of Sentiments . It called for social, civil and religious rights, including the right to vote. It took another 72 years for the 19th Amendment to become law in 1920, prohibiting the denial of voting rights on the basis of sex. In Vermont, women’s rights have come gradually. items.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
items.author: Courtenay Brown
items.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. But while soaring airfare prices seem inescapable, there may be some key ways to protect your bank account this year. Last year 81.6 million people hit the skies or the highway for Thanksgiving between Tuesday, Nov. 24, and Monday, Nov. 30. This year, the agency projects around 81.5 million Americans will do the same for a decline of 0.1% or 121,000 fewer travelers. items.title: Spartans look to exploit Tennessee's thin frontcourt in a road college basketball battle
items.summary: In any sport, the end goal is to win the championship. Every year we evaluate teams and make a list of how many could win the whole thing, and a few that might have a shot if everything goes right for them. With College Basketball , we’ve seen certain teams like Duke, UConn, and some others become part of the conversation annually. Then there are some random teams that are good, but might not be true contenders. The book includes writing on Chicago house music, the Replacements, Lucinda Williams and Wilco, alongside discussions of Prince, Motown, Tina Turner, Chicago’s Blue Note, the old Uptown Bar and more. Because so many artists contributed, the book is packed with colorful, behind-the-scenes anecdotes. New York City’s public schools lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers the Education Department released Monday. That leaves the nation’s largest school system with about 766,900 students, from kindergarten through senior year, as of Oct. 31, with several contributing factors leading to the drop: falling birth rates, families leaving the city and a slowdown of immigration into the five boroughs under President Donald Trump. Over the past decade, the city has lost about 200,000 students, or nearly 20%. Enrollment in city-funded preschool programs was up slightly, thanks to the rollout of a new program for 2,000 2-year-olds this year as well as an uptick in 4-year-olds signed up for prekindergarten programs. Released Tuesday and just weeks after Digger, the latest high-profile climate movie that features Tom Cruise as an oil tycoon, the report from the USC Annenberg School for Communications and Journalism and Good Energy, a nonprofit story consultancy, examines climate change in scripted entertainment. The report analyzes 35,120 scripts from 2021 to 2024, building on a 2022 report that found climate-related keywords in just 2.8% of scripts.

items.title: Did Oklahoma see one of the biggest leftward shifts compared to its neighboring states in the 2026 midterm election?

items.summary: Yes. A New York Times analysis comparing votes from 2026 midterm election House races to the 2024 election found that Oklahoma voters shifted Democratic +18 points, 3 more than the national average, and less than only Texas’s 19 points among neighboring states. A Democratic shift was also present at the county level; each county shifted left compared to 2024 by an average of 13 points, though Senator-elect Kevin Hern won every county except Oklahoma and Cleveland by an overall margin of 18 points. In terms of two-party vote share, Oklahoma was 18 points more Republican than the nation. This margin is notably smaller than the 34-point and 30-point margins in 2024 and 2020, respectively. items.title: Lakes Are Bizarrely Syncing Up Globally, And Scientists Are Worried

items.summary: Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage. items.summary: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years . Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status. The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world. “Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.” Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. items.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status, marking embarrassing stain on its public health record
items.author: Andrew Joseph
items.summary: International health officials said Tuesday that measles is no longer considered eliminated in the United States, a finding that was widely expected but that marks an embarrassing and avoidable backslide in the country’s basic public health standing. The announcement, made after a meeting of a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional World Health Organization body, is a largely symbolic recognition of transmission that’s already occurred. But it could have political ramifications, with resurgent Democrats already attacking the Trump administration — in particular, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — for not responding forcefully to recent outbreaks and for mixed messaging around the benefits of vaccination. Read the rest...

The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai. He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life. “I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

It all started in Switzerland, according to a source familiar with the outage. Exchange Online servers that power Outlook started to fall offline. items.title: The US has officially lost control of measles
items.author: Dylan Scott
items.summary: A healthcare worker takes down signs at a Maryland vaccine clinic. | Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images This year, the United States has recorded more measles cases — 5,739 as of Tuesday, November 17 — than in the past 25 years combined. There are active outbreaks in New York , Pennsylvania , and across the Midwest . At least eight people have died with measles infections in the US. None of this is supposed to happen in the 21st century. In 2000, the United States declared that measles had been eliminated. For years, the extremely rare cases the US saw were from people who contracted the virus in another country and brought it back to America; we didn’t have to worry about measles spreading naturally in our communities. But that’s no longer true. The Pan American Health Organization, which works with the countries in the Western Hemisphere on ongoing public health threats as well as emergency response, made it official Monday after the annual meeting of its measles and rubella elimination commission: The United States’ measles elimination status has been revoked. items.title: The death of the internet ‘built for human eyeballs’ is still ‘underappreciated’ by financial markets, UBS warns
items.author: Nick Lichtenberg
items.summary: The internet was built on a simple bet: a person is looking at the screen. UBS says AI agents are starting to break that bargain. “Since its inception, the internet has been built for human eyeballs,” Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer for the Americas at UBS Wealth Management, said in a note and podcast released Monday. “Every website, every checkout button, and every software dashboard assumes a person is sitting behind the screen, clicking through tabs.” AI agents that shop, compare and click on a person’s behalf break that assumption, she argued, and with it two of tech’s most profitable business models: digital advertising and enterprise software sold as a service. Her name for the shift: “We are moving from B2C (business to consumer) to B2A (business to agent).” And her warning to investors: “We believe the speed of AI disruption is still underappreciated by the markets.” The stakes are plain for any company whose revenue depends on a customer’s attention, or lack of it. items.title: Pantera-backed Codex raises $30 million to link Asia to global markets with stablecoins
items.author: Camila Grigera Naón
items.summary: Money might make the world go round—but that doesn’t mean getting it around the world is easy. And while stablecoins, or cryptocurrencies pegged to fiat money, can simplify the process considerably, many businesses still lack the infrastructure to use them for cross-border payments. That’s where Codex sees an opportunity. The Delaware-based startup announced Tuesday it raised $30 million in a Series A round to help businesses send money across borders and exchange currencies, without the need to deposit money in advance to use the service. Codex aims to carve out a niche in Asia and connect the region to markets in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. “We help people convert money into whatever form they want and give it to whoever they want, wherever they want,” Haonan Li, cofounder and CEO of Codex, told Fortune . “Turns out, in lots of parts of the world, this is actually super hard to do.” The 35-person company plans to use part of the capital to further automate its foreign-exchange platform, with AI agents central to its vision for how the business will operate, and keep costs down as transaction volumes grow. items.title: New math tools reveal brain activity more accurately by correcting noisy calcium signals
items.summary: When a firework bursts in the sky, what often follows is a cloud of smoke in the shape of the firework—a visual echo that lingers long after the spectacular explosion itself is over. A similar phenomenon happens in the brain when a neuron fires: The explosion of activity causes a change in calcium levels, resulting in fluorescence that neuroscientists use as a proxy for brain activity. Unfortunately, however, much like that cloud of smoke, the calcium indicator only approximates the original's shape, size and origin.

You can live in a town for years and still feel like you’re visiting. You know the streets, where to buy groceries, which restaurant you like. Belonging takes something more. For me, local music has often been how that happens. You start going to a room. You recognize a few faces. You hear someone play a song they wrote, and something in it stays with you. You come back. Eventually, you have people to say hello to, a favorite song to ask for and a friend you want to bring along. You have a place in what’s happening. When I talk about local music, I’m thinking particularly about original music: people writing songs and making records in the communities where they live. Hearing a song from its writer offers a connection you can follow. You might hear an early version, then watch it become a record. The song becomes part of your history with a place. items.title: Researchers count kinetochore proteins in living cells using an improved fluorescence-based method
items.summary: Accurate division of genetic material is critical for life and growth, and key to this is a protein structure called the kinetochore. Without this structure, the genetic material cannot be segregated equally into two daughter cells. However, challenges in discovering the exact molecular organization of the kinetochore in living cells have prevented researchers from understanding how these proteins work together to build it.

items.title: Nanogap architecture could help integrate quantum light sources onto chips
items.summary: Quantum light sources that emit light with special quantum properties, such as single photons, are critical for quantum photonic technologies, including quantum communication, computing and sensing. In this regard, monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe₂), a two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor material, hosts localized emissive states that enable light emission with sharp or narrow line widths, meaning that the emitted light has a narrow range of photon energies. This sharp luminescence makes this material a promising candidate for implementing on-chip quantum light sources.

items.title: Does locking up a student's cell phone improve test scores? A new study suggests so
items.author: Cory Turner
items.summary: Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly. The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students’ reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students’ phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses. “Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year,” says Harvard University’s Tom Kane, one of the new study’s co-authors. “It’s been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak.” Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That’s a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement. “That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” adds Dartmouth College’s Douglas Staiger, another co-author. The study’s authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. items.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
items.author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
items.summary: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

items.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.summary: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. Learning what sets off this inflammation on a cellular level could eventually help researchers find ways to stop it from becoming chronic.

items.title: Mild respiratory infections do not permanently affect immune age
items.author: Anne Gregory
items.summary: Researchers at the Leibniz Research Center for Working Environments and Human Factors Dortmund (IfADo) have investigated whether viral infections, such as the common cold or COVID-19, affect what is known as immune age, which describes how old a person's immune system is compared to their actual chronological age. In a recent study published in Immunity & Ageing, they found that, following full recovery, the immune age had not increased. Any changes observed are only temporary and form part of the natural immune response.

items.title: New findings reveal how rice blight spreads within plants and where it may stall
items.author: Arne Claussen
items.summary: The bacterial pathogen Xoo causes bacterial blight disease in rice plants that leads to substantial yield losses. Researchers from Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) have published two advances on the infection mechanisms of the pathogen in the scientific journals Phytopathology and BMC Microbiology. They established that it is unlikely that the infection spreads from the roots to shoots via contaminated water and discovered that the bacterial cells assume multicellular forms to penetrate the leaf interior from the xylem network.

items.title: Species in tropical rainforests may be surprisingly young with emergence linked to geological upheavals
items.summary: How did the rich biodiversity in the tropics originally emerge? One traditional explanation is that tropical regions have provided species with favorable habitats for millions of years. While, for example, Europe's flora and fauna have been subjected to repeated ice ages, many ancient evolutionary lineages have persisted for a long time in the tropics.

items.title: Stellar pulsations reveal hidden 1.8-solar-mass companion
items.summary: Massive stellar companions can be difficult to detect because they emit little visible light or show no obvious signs of accretion. Their gravitational pull, however, can be traced through the motion of nearby stars. In pulsating stars, regular brightness variations act as natural clocks, offering a way to find these hidden objects.

items.title: The color of uniformity: Far-red light effects on plant growth
items.summary: Ever wandered through a field of plants and observed how their heights are relatively uniform? In nature, this is partly due to plants' ability to sense their neighbors through light receptors and shade-avoidance responses. When a lower ratio of red to far-red (FR) light is detected due to the presence of neighboring plants, plants elongate their stems to compete for light.

items.title: Nvidia faces its own Lehman moment
items.author: Liz Hoffman
items.summary: The position of Nvidia’s Colette Kress — a relatively unknown CFO, a rare female executive in an industry dominated by men, promoted in a storm and taking the mic for the high-stakes earnings call this afternoon — will ring familiar to old Wall Street hands. In March 2008, the day after the Bear Stearns rescue, Lehman Brothers put Erin Callan, its finance chief of barely three months, in front of analysts to clear some blood from the water and defend Lehman’s books. She was poised and persuasive, and the stock soared. Then short seller David Einhorn started picking apart her numbers. By June, Callan was out and Lehman was in a crisis of confidence from which it wouldn’t recover. Callan became a textbook case of the “glass cliff” — women promoted into the spotlight just as things go over the edge — and disappeared from Wall Street before a reputation-mending book tour. Kress, now interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned amid a probe into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and allegations of further affairs with subordinates, faces a different test today. items.title: US data center emissions rival entire countries
items.author: Chloé Farand
items.summary: The largest data centers in the US collectively emit an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually — almost as much as Denmark, according to a study published in the journal Nature Sustainability. Harvard researchers found 403 data centers used almost 2% of US electricity , with most of the power being generated from fossil fuels. Sites in Iowa, Ohio, and Virginia accounted for about half the estimated emissions. The study provides the first peer-reviewed estimates of emissions generated by US data centers since the start of the AI boom, although it is not a comprehensive inventory. Without a publicly available list of facilities, researchers pieced together information using a commercial dataset, satellite imagery, and data on the power mix supplying each regional electricity grid. The findings are likely an underestimate as they exclude data centers that researchers could not sufficiently verify, as well as facilities that rely on on-site power generation. — Chloé Farand

items.title: Wind power's high cost-saving potential
items.author: Chloé Farand
items.summary: Adding wind power to solar and battery storage can cut the cost of meeting nearly all of global electricity demand by close to 20% , demonstrating how renewables can deliver reliable power when it is needed at low costs. Analysis by global energy think tank Ember found that the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand falls from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour when wind complements solar and batteries to generate power on short winter days and prolonged periods of cloud cover. The analysis assumes the remaining 10% is met by gas or diesel backup. In most countries, the trinity of wind, solar, and batteries reduces the need for energy storage systems, although it has little impact near the equator. It also significantly diminishes the risk of a solar and wind lull striking at the same time — a weather phenomenon often described by the German term , which refers to a dark and windless period. High costs of capital in some parts of the world, such as Africa, increase the cost of clean power, however. — Chloé Farand

At supermarkets, shoppers can buy individually portioned, ready-to-eat fillets; airports and gas stations stock premade salmon bowls. Salmon’s ascent didn’t happen by accident. When Norwegian fish breeders, farmers, and businesspeople learned to raise a wild fish in massive underwater pens, exporters worked hard to sell Americans on farmed Atlantic salmon. (They also persuaded Japanese consumers to overcome their aversion to raw salmon in sushi.) In 2025, the United States imported more than half a million metric tons of salmon—not just from Norway, but from Chile, Scotland, and other producers—and food marketers want to create yet more occasions for eating salmon, at your desk, between flights, or after a workout. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new rates will take effect on seven state-owned bridges in California's San Francisco Bay Area , according to an alert from Bay Area FasTrak. Drivers using a FasTrak toll tag will pay $9 for a standard two-axle vehicle, while those with a registered license plate account will pay $9.25. Drivers who receive an invoice in the mail will pay $10, the alert said. (The Golden Gate Bridge is not included.) The Bay Area Toll Authority (BATA) told Fox News Digital the increases are needed to maintain, repair and operate the bridges as they age. items.title: China agrees to cut some Canada tariffs
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: China agreed to cut some levies on imports from Canada, as Ottawa looks to reduce its trade reliance on the US. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hailed “ greater predictability and stability ” in relations with Beijing after talks with China’s leader Xi Jinping. Still, though Carney has made diversifying away from the US a key pillar of his trade policy, Canada’s exports to its southern neighbor have actually in recent months. Mexico’s president — who also met with Xi on Tuesday — has likewise sought to reduce her country’s dependence on Washington. But while President Donald Trump’s tariffs have upended global geopolitics, the US’ biggest trade partners are struggling to undo decades of supply chain integration. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: Fresh wave of French protests over cost of living concerns
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: French protests driven by frustration over the cost of living and public services resume today, with economists offering a bleak prognosis for one of Europe’s biggest economies. The French government is grappling with sky-high debt, a worrying deficit, and slow growth , while public anger has propelled a far-right party into the driver’s seat for 2027 presidential elections. That latter scenario is now “the key source of uncertainty,” Goldman Sachs said in a note to clients. Morgan Stanley, meanwhile, warned that while France in theory had numerous paths — to fiscal consolidation as well as fiscal crisis — “they are not equal in number and width … There is an Autobahn to wider spreads and a narrow back alley to much tighter ones.” — Prashant Rao

items.title: Global stocks fall on growing fears of a tech downturn

items.summary: Asian and European stock markets slumped amid increasing warnings over the economic fallout of a tech downturn. Bourses in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan all fell after AI stocks in the US declined yesterday. A European Central Bank vice president warned that “AI-related risks,” alongside heightened public debt levels, posed major, systemic challenges to the continent’s economies; separately, Bloomberg reported that HSBC sold part of a loan tied to a US data center project at a deep discount , highlighting worry over the financing of the AI boom. While the global economy has had “a very good run,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, it is due for “a reset of sorts.” — Prashant Rao

items.title: Trump’s team divided on China policy ahead of meeting with Xi

items.summary: The Trump administration’s division over China policy broke out into the public just days ahead of a summit between the superpowers. Trump, for his part, appears eager to avoid another trade war with Beijing, vowing to stop short of moves that could “ insult China ,” though hawks hope his words “ are merely diplomatic niceties .” Either way, the Republicans’ recent electoral blowout has constrained Trump’s room for maneuver. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: The Least Productive Day of the Year
items.author: Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic
items.summary: Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out. She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. “I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,” Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait. Rogers and her co-workers will be joined by an untold number of other players who have rearranged their lives, in ways large and small, so they can savor their first taste of this particular game. items.title: ‘Yankee Go Home’
items.author: Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic
items.summary: Introduction by Sophia Grace Carter I n September , the photojournalist Lynsey Addario traveled to Venezuela with Atlantic staff writer Anne Applebaum. They arrived in a country devastated by back-to-back earthquakes in June and still reeling from the U.S. military operation that had toppled its president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Drawing on her reporting there, Applebaum argues in The Atlantic ’s December issue that the Trump administration has revived a familiar form of Yankee imperialism, laying claim to Venezuela’s oil troves with little regard for the interests of its people. Addario’s images capture the head-spinning transformations under way—and how some citizens are chafing against the new political order and others are attempting to preserve some semblance of normalcy. [ From the December 2026 issue: Anne Applebaum on what the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela ] Addario has covered nearly every major global conflict of the past two decades—the U.S. invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, the genocide in Darfur, the civil wars in Libya and Syria, Russia’s incursion into Ukraine. items.title: The soil scientist who revolutionized organic strawberry farming in California
items.author: Liz Carlisle
items.summary: The sun was just starting to emerge through the fog at Hansen Agricultural Experiment Station as Joji Muramoto, 65, pulled two dozen soil sensors out of his SUV to set up his latest field trial. When Muramoto first came to this facility east of Oxnard some two decades ago, few people thought his organic method for controlling soilborne diseases in strawberry fields would work. Now, as the specialist for the University of California’s Cooperative Extension program lays out the final field trial before his retirement next summer, the elegant fermentation-based technique is used in at least 11 states and nine other countries — not just on strawberries but increasingly for vegetables and tree crops as well. Muramoto knelt on the soil in well-worn jeans and dug a hole for one of the sensors, measuring to be sure the bottom was precisely 9.5 inches deep. He worked with the sure-handed muscle memory of someone who’s done this thousands of times, and the urgency of someone who knew his work was not yet finished. Because affordability remains a key reason why many would-be homebuyers remain on the sidelines, builders are offering reduced mortgage rates to get people over the threshold. Americans who bought a new home paid an average starting mortgage rate of 5.01% in the third quarter, compared with a 6.15% rate for buyers of existing homes, according to a report released Tuesday by Realtor.com . Such incentives aren’t new. Many builders have long leveraged their relationships with lenders or have offered mortgage rate buydowns to help buyers during periods of high interest rates. And even if the incentives are temporary, they can add up meaningfully: Austin-based Realtor.com estimates that homebuyers could save nearly $3,100 in interest on the purchase of a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment in the first year of homeownership compared with someone buying the same-priced existing home at the average starter rates. Researchers examined 22 pancreatic tumors from patients of different racial backgrounds across the U.S., looking for differences in cancer cells and how the immune system responds to them. The study included seven Black patients and 15 non-African American patients. The findings were published in the journal Cancer Research. Some of those cell characteristics have been associated with drug resistance, but the study did not establish whether they affected patients’ treatment outcomes. Additionally, tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.

Two and a half hours later, the doula walked into Stockman’s delivery room. “I’ll never forget the coffee in her fucking hand,” Stockman told me recently. Her doula, she said, caught only the last 10 or so minutes of her labor, and she didn’t visit after the baby’s birth, as they had agreed on. Stockman said she paid $2,500 for the doula’s services: “What a waste.” Stockman is one of several women I interviewed who have had dissatisfying experiences with a birth doula, a role that makes up a fast-growing and largely unregulated part of the health-care workforce. Meet the manual treadmill, also called a self-powered or non-motorized treadmill. These machines are designed with a curved surface so that as you land from each stride, the force of your foot moving downward revolves the belt around the deck. Each step you take powers the treadmill. (There are also some flat manual treadmills, though they’re far less common and generally used only for walking.) items.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
items.author: Luca Cesari
items.summary: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food.

Less than 2% of West Virginia properties have flood insurance to protect them, according to a report released last month by the U.S. Government Accountability Office. More than a third of West Virginia properties are in high-risk flood zones. The state is second only to Louisiana for the highest proportion of high-risk properties, according to GAO’s analysis of 2024 data from climate risk analysis company First Street. The West Virginia Geographic Information System Technical Center identifies 22 West Virginia counties as being at high risk of flooding. Two people have died from flooding this year in the state, and 14 died last year. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. items.summary: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. items.title: Recounts rarely flip election results, but at least four are on tap in Minnesota
items.author: Brian Arola
items.summary: Voters shouldn’t expect recounts to change outcomes in close Minnesota races this year, but they also shouldn’t be surprised if a flip happens. After all, Minnesota has one of history’s most famous examples of it. A lengthy recount process in the 2008 U.S. Senate race resulted in Al Franken overcoming an initial 215-vote deficit against Norm Coleman. That race, however, was a clear exception. An analysis by civic nonprofit FairVote found it was one of only three reversals out of 7,437 statewide races between 2000 to 2025. Non-statewide races, where fewer votes are cast, are more likely to produce closer results. And Minnesota has multiple races where margins are theoretically close enough to make reversals possible after recounts, said Deb Otis, a researcher at FairVote. “Some of these Minnesota recounts this year really are within that margin where it’s plausible that a recount could change the outcome,” she said. “For most recounts across the country, when I talk to folks I say, ‘Hey your outcome is probably not going to change.’ You all this year are an exception.” Where are these races? The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Carden Glenn is the director of ekiM for Change , a volunteer-run public health organization that works to prevent overdoses in Greenville and surrounding rural communities. For much of the past decade, she relied on funding from the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to buy drug test strips, used to check for contaminants in the street-drug supply. But in April, the federal agency sent out a “Dear Colleague” letter announcing that organizations like hers could no longer use its money to buy test strips for fentanyl, xylazine , medetomidine, or other substances that heighten the risk of overdose, particularly when the user is unaware of what they’re consuming. Carden Glenn’s options? “Well, I’m 81 years old, and I get Social Security,” she said, “so I use my Social Security. And I’m lucky to have a husband who can support me.” She also has other retirement income; she allocates that to ekiM’s work as well. Occasionally, she receives a donation. A new directive could bring faith leaders into a greater public role in policy-making and advisement to state leaders. For virtually the entirety of Delaware’s history, the state’s faith leaders have played a role in social change. The famed Peter Spencer founded the African Union Church in Wilmington, challenging racial exclusion in Methodist congregations of the early 1800s. Thomas Garrett, a white Quaker abolitionist, helped thousands of escaped slaves make their way to freedom on the Underground Railroad. And the Rev. Maurice Moyer, a Black Presbyterian minister from Wilmington, led the city’s NAACP chapter during the height of the civil rights movement in the early 1960s. Today, many churches serve as service providers for Delaware’s homeless population and have advocated against gun violence and police misconduct. Earlier this year, Gov. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. Crowd disorder before kickoff in a poorly maintained, badly policed venue resulted in the deaths of 39 fans. In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Hospice-ct.jpg" /> Elisabeth Kübler-Ross was born 100 years ago this past July. She is remembered, almost entirely, for five words: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. They make up a model of grief so thoroughly absorbed into the culture that it now turns up in sports commentary and breakup advice. The five stages made her famous, but another lasting legacy of hers took root in Connecticut. A never-published letter from her archives shows how the ambitions she shared with a Yale nursing dean helped give the country its first hospice, and how far American end-of-life care still has to go. Earlier this year, her family shared with me a letter she typed on Jan. 1, 1971, to Dame Cicely Saunders, the British physician who had opened St. Christopher’s Hospice in London four years earlier. The secret agent has nearly always been played by an up-and-coming, well-regarded talent who looks good in a tux. So for years, as the debate has dragged on over who would replace Daniel Craig in the role, dozens of names along those lines have bubbled up; these most recently included Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor. Some possible candidates aged out of the role while waiting for it to open up, in the same way that potential popes find themselves hitting retirement age before their chance at the papacy arrives. But the final choice for the new Bond, Robert Pattinson, completely defies that established logic: By casting someone who’s already globally popular, the franchise is somehow taking the risky version of a typically very safe bet. Pattinson makes plenty of sense on paper as Bond: He’s about the right age (he turned 40 this year) and the right height, at 6 foot 1; he’s debonair and British in all the appreciable ways; he wears a suit better than anyone. items.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.author: Scott K. Johnson
items.summary: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

items.summary: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search . Read full article Comments

items.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
items.author: Eric Berger
items.summary: The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. Read full article Comments

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. California’s attorney general is suing OpenAI, saying a high-profile cybersecurity incident could have been avoided had the company installed proper safeguards. items.summary: There is a considerable delay from prescription of biologic therapy to final approval for pediatric patients, and almost 40% of prescriptions requiring a prior authorization (PA) are denied, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, held from Nov. 12 to 16 in Phoenix.

items.title: CAR T-cell therapy shows promise for patients with lupus
items.summary: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy is associated with consistent reductions in disease activity, according to research presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR Convergence 2026), held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

items.title: Daytime brain waves resembling deep sleep could explain hallucinations in Parkinson's disease
items.summary: Parkinson's disease is a progressive brain disorder that damages dopamine-producing neurons, causing symptoms to worsen over time. The disease is associated with motor difficulties that can manifest as tremors, stiffness, poor balance and slow movements. However, the disease reaches beyond movement, affecting how people think, perceive the world around them and sleep. Caregivers and health care workers often report that cognitive decline, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and perceptual distortions add to the burden of the disease and can take the greatest toll on quality of life.

items.title: Liver cells activate scarring-linked genes in stiff surroundings but favor repair signals in softer conditions
items.summary: Soft and stiff extracellular matrix environments influence how hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) respond during liver injury. Researchers from Science Tokyo investigated how matrix stiffness shapes the direction of HSC activation. They revealed that soft conditions favored regeneration-associated cellular states, while stiff conditions promoted fibrosis-associated gene expression.

items.title: US set to lose measles-free certification
items.summary: This week, the United States will lose its designation as a country where measles has been eliminated, as an outbreak of the dangerous, highly contagious disease keeps spreading.

items.title: No oxygen? Chicken brain cells still survive
items.author: Amber Veverka
items.summary: Without oxygen, brain cells die within minutes … or do they? When it's a chicken brain, Wake Forest University researcher Lara do Amaral-Silva has found, the answer is no.

items.title: More than half of physician disciplinary actions in California study involved gaps in medical knowledge
items.summary: Gaps in medical knowledge, such as prescribing inappropriate medications, incorrectly interpreting imaging studies or ordering an unnecessary high-risk procedure that could jeopardize a patient's health, played a role in 52.3% of the physician disciplinary actions reviewed in a new American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) study published in the Journal of Continuing Education in the Health Professions.

items.title: Researchers find potential way to protect the brain from HIV and opioid damage
items.summary: People living with HIV continue to struggle with memory loss, difficulty concentrating and poor decision-making, even as antiretroviral treatments have dramatically improved life expectancy. For patients who also use opioids—which may be prescribed to manage the chronic pain that can accompany HIV—these cognitive problems can be even worse. Until now, scientists haven't understood exactly why.

items.title: Scientists identify likely cause of typhoid fever's deadliest complication
items.summary: Typhoid fever is an ancient scourge that remains all too deadly in the developing world today. And while it has been described in detail for more than a century, the reasons for its lethality have never been understood. Yale researchers now have an answer.

items.title: 32 Americans named as Rhodes scholars have variety of interests, from space junk to art history
items.author: Associated Press
items.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare are among the 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars. The winners, who were announced on Saturday, have a variety of interests, from bioelectronics to water scarcity to art history. They were chosen from 238 finalists who emerged from more than 1,000 candidates who received formal endorsements from their colleges and universities for the honor. The students will attend the University of Oxford in England as part of the Rhodes scholar program, which awards more than 100 scholarships worldwide each year for students to pursue two to three years of graduate studies. Two students are the first-ever Rhodes scholars from their schools — Prairie View A&M University in Texas and The Citadel — The Military College of South Carolina. Harvard University led the way with four 2027 Rhodes scholars, followed by Yale and Princeton with three each. The winners include: Evan Garrison Credit: Emily Grace McCall Evan Garrison, of Webb City, Missouri, a senior at Mississippi State University majoring in aerospace engineering and mathematics. items.title: Insurance commissioner mulls one-time grants as more Mississippians drop health coverage
items.author: Gwen Dilworth
items.summary: Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney is considering a proposal he says could help Mississippians struggling to afford health coverage. Chaney told Mississippi Today his office is weighing a proposal to provide one-time grants of about $250 to help low-income people without health insurance pay for healthcare expenses. The program would be funded through the Mississippi Comprehensive Health Insurance Risk Pool Association, the state’s long-dormant insurer of last resort. The grants could be used to buy a health insurance plan, offset an emergency room bill, see a primary care physician or pay for a flu shot. “This is not about socialism,” Chaney said. “It’s about keeping people out of the ER and keeping them healthy so you have a healthy workforce.” Chaney’s proposition underscores the challenges of many low-income Mississippians struggling to afford healthcare costs. Mississippi has been hit particularly hard by the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act tax subsidies last December. Those tax credits had made health insurance more affordable for tens of thousands of Mississippians. They will be made available to the public on the Mississippi Electronic Court system on Dec. 7. Smith sealed the court filings after he canceled a hearing in May , when public officials were set to testify on the chain of custody of the missing evidence. The evidence ranged from a rape kit to fingernail scrapings to a strip of tape, and was tied to a rape and manslaughter appeal by King Brown Jr. Brown was convicted in 2005 after a third trial of the rape and killing of a 6-year-old Greenville girl. items.title: Man said he asked questions about Nolan Wells case, then was jailed
items.author: Mina Corpuz

People on social media are calling out a lack of transparency about his arrest. The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department took Christian Anthony Claudio, 25, into custody after his extradition from Otsego County New York on Saturday. By Monday morning, department officials listed him on its jail docket with a felony charge of making terroristic threats. In an affidavit in Jackson County Court uploaded Monday afternoon, Claudio is accused of threatening to travel to Mississippi to kill chancery court clerks “due to findings of a high profile death investigation.” He had a first appearance in Jackson County where his bond was set at $50,000, and one of his bond conditions was to stop posting about the case on social media. items.title: National Folk Festival welcomes diverse cultures and entertainment to downtown Jackson
items.author: Simeon Gates
items.summary: The 83rd National Folk Festival brought visitors, art and traditional culture from the Deep South and beyond to downtown Jackson over the weekend. The free, three-day event allowed festivalgoers to enjoy three food courts, six stages and over 300 artists, including performers, craftspeople and some food vendors. Visitors could shop from a marketplace of artists and craftspeople from across the Deep South. One such artist is Kai Mosley, a Hattiesburg-based self-taught mixed-media artist, writer and illustrator who owns the brand Existential Cowboy . Mosley’s wares included stickers, prints, paintings and more. It was Mosley’s first time at a big market, and she was eager to connect with people in real life. “I really love Mississippi, and I love that it’s bringing people from around the country to Mississippi and seeing what we have to offer,” said Mosely, whose booth was among the many set up on a closed Capitol Street in front of the Governor’s Mansion. items.title: Retrial in New Albany stabbing will proceed
items.author: Mina Corpuz
items.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court declined Monday to consider double jeopardy issues raised in the case of a north Mississippi man whom a judge acquitted of attempted murder and is set to be retried . Attorneys for Lane Mitchell asked the nation’s high court last month to hear his case, arguing that a 5-4 Mississippi Appeals Court decision violated their client’s protection from being tried twice for the same charge. Mitchell’s case was one of over a 100 petitions for review denied without explanation by the court. Typically, the U.S. Supreme Court accepts very few requests for review. Before the high court considered the petition, parents of the victim, Russell Rogers, shared their concerns about how the case was presented to the justices, including how it contained what they called misstatements. In 2019, Mitchell , then 18, stabbed Rogers of Collierville, Tennessee, at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany, believing the man posed a threat to his father, who was working as a bartender, and to a female waitress. After an incident where a “contractor removed a pump” at SpaceXSI’s facility at 8235 Tulane Road in Southaven, the company allowed 5,000 to 6,000 gallons of a propylene glycol mixture to spill into a neighboring drainage ditch, state officials told Mississippi Today on Monday. items.title: When a pro-ICE film came to town, Livingston wasn’t ready
items.author: Nick Mott
items.summary: This story also appeared in High Country News The film shoot, to folks living nearby, seemed to emerge out of nowhere. In late September, orange-and-white traffic barricades shut down a normally quiet residential street east of the neon lights and brick facades of Livingston, Montana’s picturesque downtown. Cameras began rolling and actors dressed as Antifa rioters and U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement officers began firing blank rounds. The film crew eventually blew up a car. The less literal explosions that followed weren’t confined to the closed streets, or even to Livingston. Soon, real-life protesters demonstrated against the movie, while extras portraying activists rioted on set. As cameras rolled, a private security team wielding functional weapons patrolled the street closures. Passersby observed the filming through the set’s barricades, many seemingly perplexed. The movie — working title Pawn Shop — became politicized across the globe as both supporters and detractors of the film railed about the conflict on social media. items.title: State Farm To Pay $45 Million After Oklahoma Insurance Investigation
items.author: Paul Monies
items.summary: State Farm Fire and Casualty Co. will pay a $45 million settlement after a state insurance department investigation found it failed to properly pay roof damage claims by Oklahoma customers. The state’s incoming insurance commissioner, Republican Bob Sullivan, said he was still learning details on Friday but worried the settlement may take some flexibility out of any regulatory approach to State Farm under his administration. The settlement calls for the Illinois-based insurance company, which has been the focus of hundreds of lawsuits , to let customers with wind and hail damage ask for an independent review if they had claims closed without payment from 2021 to 2025. State Farm is Oklahoma’s top homeowners insurer, with more than 258,000 customers and $785.9 million in homeowners premiums in 2025. Its state market share in that category is more than 30%. State Farm’s settlement includes at least $35 million for customer claims. The company will pay $10 million for new grants under the Insurance Department’s Strengthen Oklahoma Homes program. items.title: The expanding genetics of blue eyes in cats
items.summary: Blue eyes in cats have long attracted attention, especially when they occur in cats with fully colored coats. The dominant blue eye (DBE) phenotype has become increasingly visible across several breeds. When we prepared our literature review, four independent DBE variants had been described in scientific publications. Today, eight variants are reported, although published genetic evidence is available for six. Some of these variants are also associated with health concerns.

items.title: Why marine climate refugia matter for safeguarding the world's oceans
items.summary: The ocean is changing rapidly. Warming, acidification, oxygen loss, sea-level rise and the intensification of extreme events are transforming marine ecosystems, leading to species shifts and mass mortality events. However, these impacts are not distributed evenly. There are areas that buffer these effects and act as true "marine climate refugia."

items.title: Ultracold diamond microwave laser amplifies quantum signals 1,000-fold
items.summary: Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have created a spin-based microwave amplifier that operates near absolute zero, boosting signals by more than 1,000-fold while adding noise close to the bare minimum required by the laws of physics. As a more robust alternative to current state-of-the-art devices, the OIST device can handle much stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, paving the way for practical quantum computing and higher-resolution sensing technologies.

items.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
items.author: Max G. Levy
items.summary: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded

items.title: Undocumented students no longer eligible for SEED scholarship at DelTech
items.author: Julia Merola
items.summary: Why Should Delaware Care? The Student Excellence Equals Degree, or SEED, scholarship was established more than 20 years ago to expand access to education at the Delaware Technical Community College. Earlier this fall, the college changed the interpretation of a Delaware resident to exclude undocumented students. The decision marked the end of one of few scholarship opportunities for undocumented students in Delaware. A scholarship open to Delaware Technical Community College students who had attended high school in the state is no longer available to undocumented immigrants. The change in eligibility for the SEED scholarship — which effectively allows a student to attend DelTech tuition-free — was to align with federal law, a college spokesperson said. Kate Bailey, the DelTech spokesperson, told Spotlight Delaware that federal laws limit undocumented immigrants’ eligibility for “preferential treatment” programs. Although local dollars fund the SEED scholarship, she said the “law applies to any benefit based on residency,” not just those funded by the federal government. DENMARK — Following months of extended public hearings and informational sessions, the Select Board will begin deliberations this week on a request from Poland Spring to renew its water extraction permit for another five years. On Nov. 10, the Select Board closed a series of public hearings , wrapping up a process that started back in June and included multiple hearings, two postponements and written questions from residents that were later answered by Poland Spring. The board will begin deliberating the permit renewal for Poland Spring’s Cold Spring site at a special meeting at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 18. That meeting is scheduled to continue on Nov. 24 and possibly Dec. 1, with a decision expected at the regular meeting scheduled for Dec. 8, with written findings due within 30 days of that meeting. The bottled water company is allowed to take up to 432,000 gallons of water per day — or 105.1 million gallons per year — under the town’s water extraction ordinance and annual monitoring report. items.author: Simmone Shah
items.summary: An aerial shows a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction on Oct. 29, 2026 in Vernon, California. —Mario Tama—Getty Images America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability . The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models , has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers . American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. items.author: Katy Sherman
items.summary: —Michael Sugrue—Getty Images What followed that day is a blurry haze. When I try to remember specifics, it plays in my mind like quick cuts in a television show: A kind resident swabbing my cervix calmly, but then returning to the triage room with a larger group of doctors, all with somber faces. A fast transfer to a labor and delivery room. A steroid shot for my baby’s lungs and a magnesium drip for his brain; IV antibiotics and a fetal monitor. Our son, holding on. We made it to 24 hours after my water broke without delivering—a critical milestone, we were told—before I was transferred to the antepartum wing. items.title: Forced drug switches are burying clinics in paperwork
items.author: Teresa Fama
items.summary: This commentary is by Teresa Fama, a practicing rheumatologist at University of Vermont Health. Vermont and the nation are struggling with how to reduce healthcare costs. Much of the increase is due to prescription drugs and labor, particularly as the latter makes up 65% of UVM Health’s total expenses . To highlight the compounding effect on costs from these two aspects of healthcare, let’s look at Vermont’s Act 193 . Vermont’s Act 193 requires pharmacists to dispense the lowest-priced interchangeable biologic medication to patients. These interchangeable biologic medications are biosimilars of the reference product, meaning they are highly similar with no clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity or potency — think similar to “generic.” Act 193 was enacted in 2018 when not many biosimilars were available. For example, Humira, the most prescribed biologic to treat rheumatoid arthritis, had three biosimilars approved in 2018. Today, there are 10. Act 193 was intended to reduce the cost of healthcare by reducing prescription drug prices. If passed, it would be the second bipartisan effort to honor Parton since her death. Nashville’s airport is already in the process of being renamed Dolly Parton International Airport. items.title: How an AI Content Mill Put a Real Musician Through Copyright Hell
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.summary: When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors. “Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said. Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems. During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud , where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years. Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video.
