items.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
items.author: Ben Geman
items.summary: Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data. Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy. Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states. Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs. The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited. Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. items.title: Elderly people are buying Teslas for the ‘full self-driving.’ This is a problem
items.author: David Zipper
items.summary: After retiring a few years ago, my parents moved into a wooded retirement community in North Carolina. One of their neighbors is a former physician, now in his 90s, who sensed that his reflexes had deteriorated. He no longer trusted himself behind the wheel, but he valued the independence that a car can provide. His solution: Get a Tesla. He now relies on Full Self-Driving (Supervised), Tesla’s driver assistance system, to get around. That decision is a dubious one at best. Tesla’s driver assistance system is just that: technology that can make the act of driving less onerous, but cannot replace it. A person operating Full Self-Driving (Supervised)—let’s call it FSD—must be able to intervene immediately if the system makes a mistake, which does happen . If not, their use of FSD endangers themselves along with everyone else on the road. My parents’ neighbor is far from alone. A quick scan of Facebook or TikTok reveals numerous adults with declining health who depend on FSD to keep driving. items.title: Nearly half of Americans are making the same gamble with their holiday travel plans
items.author: Sarah Bregel
items.summary: Air travel is getting more and more expensive. And as prices continue to soar, American travelers are becoming desperate for deals on flights. Oftentimes, they’re even delaying bookings or totally altering holiday travel in order to score reasonably priced plane tickets. The findings come from a new report from the online travel agency and flight consolidator CheapOair, which surveyed 1,000 U.S. consumers to understand how travelers are making decisions around holiday travel promotions. The survey found that modern day fliers are more willing to book flights at the last minute, often waiting for promotions that happen on Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Travel Tuesday. In fact, nearly half (49%) of the survey’s respondents said they have delayed bookings in order to shop holiday travel deals. Another 60% say they are likely to consider doing so in the future. Still, while fliers are perhaps more deal-driven than ever before, they’re not consistently convinced that they’ll be able to find true savings. items.title: Minnesota State has struggled to fix its finances for over a decade. Will this time be different?
items.author: Cleo Krejci
items.summary: When Minnesota State Chancellor Scott Olson pictures the financial future of the state’s largest higher education system, he sees the Titanic headed for an iceberg. The iceberg is a nearly $100 million budget shortfall, which projections suggest the 26-college and seven-university system could reach by summer 2028. “We can see it coming,” Olson told employees last month at Century College. “If we do nothing,” Olson said, the system “will find itself in insolvency.” The financial challenges have long been a problem. System officials attribute them to insufficient state funding, declining enrollment and inflation. Now they are weighing what would be the most substantial reorganization in three decades, including possible campus mergers or closures and the centralization of services like IT or financial aid. Initial proposals are expected as soon as January. One solution already approved is to take up to $25 million away from most schools, especially community colleges, to help financially struggling four-year schools . items.title: Democrats are within reach of neutering the Electoral College’s role in presidential elections
items.author: Nathaniel Rakich, Votebeat
items.summary: This article was originally published by Votebeat , a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. It’s one of the first things you learn if you take high school civics: The national popular vote doesn’t pick the president. The Electoral College does. But there’s a movement afoot to rewrite those lesson plans. And after this month’s elections, its goal — to effectively eliminate the Electoral College — may actually be within reach. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact seeks to solve a simple problem: Sometimes, the winner of the presidential election isn’t the candidate who got the most votes. There have been four times in U.S. history (1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016) when one candidate won the national popular vote but another candidate won the Electoral College — and thus became president. Those elections were followed by calls to abolish the Electoral College — usually from Democrats, who coincidentally were on the losing end of all four. But the Electoral College is written into the Constitution , so ending it would be a very heavy lift. It would require either a constitutional amendment … or a more creative solution like the NPVIC.

items.title: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
items.author: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
items.summary: The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago. Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion last week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States. “It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.” Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread. items.summary: Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. items.title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
items.author: MICHAEL CASEY
items.summary: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died. Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson. “It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” said Diane Johnson, 72. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.” Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn’t hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane. “While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship. Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. items.title: Lawsuit alleges jail staff abused Josephine County inmate during a mental health crisis
items.author: Justin Higginbottom
items.summary: A former inmate has sued Josephine County in federal court, claiming he faced abuse in jail during a psychiatric crisis. Sephiran Roberts was arrested on charges of theft in 2024. His complaint notes he has a history of serious mental illness. Instead of adequate medical care, Roberts alleges he was restrained for up to 12 hours a day with a full-body straitjacket known as “the wrap.” Roberts had attempted suicide in the jail previously and had shown destructive behavior, according to the lawsuit. The complaint also alleges jail staff beat and used a Taser on Roberts — who developed open sores on his wrists — while preventing access to his attorney and legal documents. Josephine County did not respond to requests for comment. David Boyer, an attorney with Disability Rights Oregon and representing Roberts, said many Oregon jails lack adequate mental health resources. “We’re seeing it in jails around the state,” Boyer said. He said effective treatment would have lessened Roberts’ symptoms. “Just the minimum level of mental health and medical care would have prevented all of this restraint,” Boyer said. items.title: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
items.author: Imogen Foulkes
items.summary: Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as ‘killer robots’ are underway at the United Nations in Geneva. Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week’s U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late. Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously. In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being ‘hunted’ by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans. Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week’s meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world’s dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week. items.title: United Airlines says it resolved a technology issue that affected departing flights
items.author: Ashley Landis
items.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop. Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. The airlines also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.” United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media. Pilots reported to air traffic controllers that the problem was related to United’s system that helps them determine a plane’s final weight to ensure it can safely take off. United did not immediately provide details about which of the airlines systems were affected. A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.summary: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.summary: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

items.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?
items.author: Kathryn Hulick
items.summary: AI worms aren't real-world threats yet. But tests show they can adapt and spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting each device's weaknesses.

items.title: Advocates dub midterms the ‘care election’
items.author: Eleanor Mueller
items.summary: This month’s midterms were the “care election,” according to a sweeping new report by Care Can’t Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor . The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout — citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach — as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care. “There’s this undeniable sense of momentum,” leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is “looking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.” Seven in 10 voters said it’s important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action. Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government “immediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,” including by tackling child care. Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 9

items.title: AI makes everyone more vulnerable, AT&T CEO says
items.author: Ellen DiMauro
items.summary: Everybody is more vulnerable because of AI, at least for now, AT&T CEO John Stankey said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Stankey believes that can be turned around to make things safer, but it will take some time to figure out “how to turn that technology into advantage rather than liability.” Stankey said he is by no means a “doomer” when it comes to AI, but it’s hard for anyone to know what the true full effect of these AI models will be. He added that “anxiety levels are pretty high right now” because of the added cybersecurity risks brought on by artificial intelligence. While there’s been a lot of concern around data centers and the public reaction to them, Stankey urged consideration of the downstream effects. If “a metropolitan area doesn’t have power for a period of time, or we start seeing cell phones drop from the network,” Stankey said. “We’ve got to make sure we’re doing the right things to prevent that from happening.” We can’t have “technology for technology’s sake,” he said. “If the public loses trust, if an economy is interrupted, and it can’t transact business in the way it should transact business and grow, then we’ve got technology that is built o

items.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
items.author: J.D. Capelouto
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. items.title: Bill Ackman says it’s ‘unlikely’ he’ll get involved to bring Huang back
items.author: J.D. Capelouto
items.summary: Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said Monday it was “unlikely” that he would get directly involved in an effort to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Ackman, an outspoken activist investor who runs Pershing Square Capital Management, has come to Huang’s defense following the revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Ackman acknowledged that the situation presents “a pretty interesting activist setup.” There’s still legal uncertainty about what exactly happened, Ackman told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, but if Huang’s missteps were a “personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” While “truth is pretty darn important,” he said a board should treat a CEO lying about a personal matter differently from lying about something that could endanger the company’s business. If he were running a comeback campaign, Ackman said he would “present the facts, and you call a special meeting.” Huang would have heft: Having co-founded the company, he still owns more than 3% of Nvidia. — J.D. Capelouto

items.title: Binance chief acknowledges hack ‘shouldn’t have happened’
items.author: Rohan Goswami
items.summary: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng acknowledged Monday that the $6.3 billion hack his firm suffered — one which roiled cryptocurrency markets and raised existential questions about industry security — resulted from the company’s own failings. “It shouldn’t have happened,” Teng said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “This was a multi-month, sophisticated campaign,” he continued, referring to the attack, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. (Pyongyang has denied involvement in the hack.) The hack raised questions about what is fundamentally the weakest link in most cybersecurity and business operations: humans themselves. Binance said that it was compromised in part because of a sophisticated phishing attempt that involved a Binance employee undergoing a fictitious interview process that resulted in “malicious software” being loaded onto a corporate machine, Teng noted. Teng also acknowledged Binance’s checkered reputation, involving billions in fines for anti-money laundering violations and the imprisonment of its primary shareholder and founder Changpeng Zhao. “We had really underinvested into the area of compliance,” Teng said. “Since the record fine and settlement, we hav

items.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
items.author: Alexis Akwagyiram
items.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. items.title: North Korea outreach in the mix for Trump’s Asia swing
items.author: Shelby Talcott
items.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia may include a sitdown with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Though Trump floated that possibility today, telling reporters that Kim “might come,” one senior US official said days ago that there are “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.” The White House declined to comment further on the prospect, pointing to Trump’s earlier comments. While the president met with Kim during his first term, he has yet to organize a second-term meeting. Trump’s trip will culminate with an unprecedented trilateral meeting between the US, China, and Russia. Trump is not expected to discuss Ukraine at that sitdown, the senior US official said. Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are instead expected to discuss “the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. — Shelby Talcott

items.title: Replit CEO calls Huang’s ouster ‘attack’ on open models

items.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia’s CEO “an attack on open models” at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. “Jensen is the premier champion of open models,” Masad told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami. “If it wasn’t for Jensen, there wouldn’t be a lot of funding going into US open model companies like Reflection and others.” Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Masad, who founded Replit, an AI app and website-building company, has championed the push to reinstate Huang. When a friend told him about a petition on Replit calling for the fallen CEO’s return, “I literally jumped in and did tech support for them,” Masad said. Huang has been “a great voice on pushing back on the narrative that we need to lock down AI, that the only safe AI is a closed AI,” Masad said. items.title: Trump's former AI czar criticizes rush to judgment on ex-Nvidia CEO
items.author: Jake Angelo
items.summary: President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, argued on Monday the public was too quick to judge former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though he stopped short of saying whether the board should reinstate Huang as CEO. “You have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in a proper court of law,” Sacks, a longtime venture capitalist and co-founder of Craft Ventures, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. Sacks went on to say that the public “should wait until there’s a proper determination by a legal authority” on the allegations against Huang. The Trump administration and Congress have launched investigations related to the controversy. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week following revelations that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset as well as an Nvidia employee who had reported directly to him, sending shockwaves throughout Silicon Valley. Huang acted as a linchpin of the AI trade, deploying nearly $99 billion across the tech ecosystem to fuel the AI infrastructure buildout. items.title: US tech extends slide ahead of Nvidia earnings
items.author: Brendan Ruberry
items.summary: US tech extended its slide Monday as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 5%, as investors looked ahead to the chipmaker’s first post-Jensen Huang earnings report and Anthropic’s IPO. Chip stocks sank overall after the US rolled out interim rules to close the so-called remote access loophole by which Chinese AI firms accessed cutting-edge US-made chips via third-country data centers , adding to weeks of volatility in the AI trade. Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that the pullback was driven in large part by investors being more selective about their allocations ; they have so far not had to make “hard choices,” The Wall Street Journal wrote. “ That ‘no-brainer’ era is over .” — Brendan Ruberry

items.title: STAT+: FDA approves new breast cancer drug, providing new option for some patients, boost for Roche
items.author: Andrew Joseph
items.summary: The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved a new breast cancer drug from Roche, teeing up the launch of a medicine that the Swiss company has said could become its top-selling product ever. The approval of Wilserdly, also known as giredestrant, was one of the most important regulatory decisions Roche had been awaiting. It also gives the company another foothold in breast cancer treatments, a field in which it has a storied history with the drug Herceptin through its subsidiary Genentech, though in recent years it’s fallen behind rival pharma companies in oncology. The approval is specifically for patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that has picked up a mutation in the ESR1 gene, a sign that the tumor is developing resistance to standard treatments. The evERA trial showed that the drug, an oral treatment known as a selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD, extended the time period before patients’ tumors progressed. items.title: STAT+: In a win for MAHA, FDA creates new regulatory category for the supplement NAC
items.author: Margaret Manto
items.summary: WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is proposing a new classification for a product that’s existed in a legal gray area for years, a win for proponents of dietary supplements, including members of the MAHA movement. The proposed rule would classify N-acetyl-L-cysteine, known as NAC and already widely sold over the counter, as the agency’s first “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” — in essence, not not a supplement. The need for the legal backbending stems from the fact that the FDA previously approved NAC as a drug, and FDA regulations prohibit the agency from including approved drugs in the dietary supplement category. In 1963, the agency approved NAC to break up mucus in certain lung conditions, and in 1985 to treat acetaminophen overdose. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: STAT+: Helus’ psychedelic drug improved depression in study but faces safety questions
items.author: Elaine Chen
items.summary: A psychedelic drug candidate from Helus Pharma significantly helped people with major depression in a Phase 3 trial, the company said Monday, but a number of serious adverse events in the study raised questions about the safety of the treatment. Participants took one dose of the drug, called HLP003, on the first day of the trial and a second dose three weeks later. Six weeks into the study, people taking the drug in addition to their standard antidepressants experienced a reduction of 19.5 points on a depression rating scale called the MADRS, while the placebo group had a 11.9-point reduction. At 12 weeks, the effect was largely maintained, with the treatment group seeing a 16.9-point reduction and the placebo group experiencing a 9.9-point reduction. The differences between the two groups were all statistically significant. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: STAT+: NIAID acting head John Powers III appointed as the permanent director
items.author: Anil Oza
items.summary: The acting director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, John Powers III, will become the permanent director, the agency announced Monday. NIAID has been without a permanent director since March 2025, when the Trump administration ousted Jeanne Marrazzo . Powers has been serving in an acting capacity since June . A physician-scientist, Powers has worked with NIAID since 1999 in several roles focused on clinical research. The second Trump administration has brought a renewed spotlight to the infectious disease institute, in large part because of the president’s ire for former director Anthony Fauci, and because of unsubstantiated accusations that research funded by an institute in China played a role in creating the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It has also seen tumult in its leadership. After Marrazzo was ousted, Jeffery Taubenberger was appointed acting director. He unexpectedly stepped down , and several other leaders at NIAID were reassigned to other institutes or asked to resign . Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: STAT+: Federal judge issues final ruling blocking U.S. plan to limit visa length for grad students, postdocs
items.author: Anil Oza
items.summary: A proposal by the Trump administration to cap the amount of time foreign students and scholars can spend in the country has been struck down in court. In a Monday ruling , Boston federal Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV wrote that the rule “is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law.” Saylor previously blocked the rule temporarily on the day before the policy was set to take effect. Monday’s ruling is a final decision on the case, though an appeal from the government on the initial ruling is still pending. Universities and research advocates worried that the four-year cap on visas could deter international students from pursuing graduate studies in the U.S., because such degrees often take longer than four years. items.title: STAT+: Expert warns of battleground over global access to newer GLP-1 drugs for obesity
items.author: Ed Silverman
items.summary: Over the past few months, lower-cost generic versions of the blockbuster GLP-1 drug semaglutide, which is sold as Wegovy by Novo Nordisk for combating obesity, started to become available in some countries and will soon arrive in still others. Meanwhile, the pharmaceutical industry is racing to develop newer GLP-1 medicines that, to varying degrees, are forecast to be more effective, cause fewer side effects, and are easier to administer. items.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
items.author: Sudhi Sinha
items.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. items.title: The Future of AI Is Not China
items.author: Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic. Source: Getty.
items.summary: Nathan Chen, a teenage tech prodigy, was a leading innovator at Moonshot AI, one of several top Chinese labs that have sparked fears in Silicon Valley that China is gaining ground in the race for AI supremacy. But last month, Chen posted on X that he had left the Beijing-based company. He is now at Discovery Loop, a new Palo Alto–based AI start-up with a growing stable of high-profile talent. Perhaps Chen sensed that the most exciting advances in AI were not happening in China—despite the fact that the technology’s rollout in the United States has lately looked more troubled than ever. Newly empowered Democrats, ushered to midterm victories thanks in part to public opposition to data centers, are calling to rein in construction plans. items.title: The Rise of the Fusion Democrat
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Source: iStock / Getty.
items.summary: Y ou could use practically any synonym for big to describe this month’s Democratic wins. I’ll go with staggering . For the first time in 145 years, Mississippi will have a Black senator. Roughly three-quarters of the nation’s population will now be led by Democratic governors. In the House, the Democrats expect a roomy 80-plus-seat margin over Republicans. Latinos? Young men? Working-class white people? On Election Day, they all moved left. Obviously, the Democrats are delighted. Naturally, they are also fighting. Moderates would like to take credit for this turn in the party’s fortunes, especially in red states. The rest of the online-shopping economy is also turning to EVs: The U.S. Postal Service is rolling out all-electric mail trucks, as are its private-sector rivals, like FedEx. IKEA delivers most of its modular furniture in electric vans and trucks. items.title: One Word to Explain America
items.author: Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic. Source: Getty.
items.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. I n May 2020 , as COVID-19 besieged America, Jim Justice, then the Republican governor of West Virginia, held a televised press conference. “I encourage all businesses that are allowed to open to do so only if they fuckin’ follow the guidelines to keep West Virginians safe,” he said. Social-media users across the nation were quick to celebrate, or mock, the governor’s directive. Justice swiftly claimed that the bad word in question was the result of an audio glitch, calling it a “word that I would never say nor have I ever said.” It was a technical difficulty, not a human one. Now you hear it; now you don’t. Justice may in fact have stumbled verbally , resulting in an inadvertent F-bomb. Either way, the subsequent hoopla marked a revealing and absurd crossroads in the history of American English. For many Americans, purity of tongue remains a benchmark of godliness, decency, and social order. Bad words symbolize the opposite: corruption and shame and a symptom of national distress. items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.author: Sam Leith
items.summary: Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14. So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

items.title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
items.author: Temi Wilkey
items.summary: Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost . The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died. Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough for there to be a word for it is proof of the long since disintegrated fabric of our society. items.title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

The company, Tom Health, is being spun out of Lumeris, a value-based care firm the Doerr brothers helped found. The firm launched 15 years ago, based largely off of ideas that Tom, a physician, had. Lumeris has raised more than $620 million and employs 1,200 people, according to Pitchbook. “He brought passion for quality care for every individual and inspired the company to such a degree that, without any of my involvement, they decided to name their AI after him,” Doerr said. “Tom always wanted to make health care more personal, and he wanted to give doctors more time to be doctors, all with the aim of serving patients,” he added. “In fact, he would give all of his patients his mobile phone number, and they knew they could call him any time to get him.” Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
items.author: Naoki Nitta
items.summary: Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . items.title: The chain-reaction era: Constant shock and awe
items.author: Jim VandeHei
items.summary: It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal , and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week. This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture. Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality. Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly. We call this post-processable velocity : Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb. People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?" Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators , cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger. What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. items.summary: The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds. Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth. The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios. The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going. Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy. items.title: How America can win the AI race without burning voters
items.summary: One of the biggest losers on Election Day was the AI industry. Across the country, voters delivered a clear warning about the rapid expansion of data centers powering artificial intelligence. Americans want technological progress, but not at the expense of their communities, electricity bills, water supplies or quality of life. According to Ballotpedia, 46 of the 47 data-center-related ballot measures decided in 2026 favored greater limits on development. The message is unmistakable: The industry is losing public confidence, and political leaders who ignore these concerns do so at their own peril. America needs more data centers, not fewer, to maintain its AI leadership. But technology companies cannot expect communities to welcome projects when residents believe they are absorbing the costs while corporations reap the benefits. items.summary: Rural counties swung more than 15 percentage points toward Democrats in the 2026 midterms . Republicans lost rural strongholds including Iowa, South Carolina, and Kansas, where a Democrat won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1932. Republicans haven’t fully lost rural America, but they got one heck of a warning. Just before the election, a national survey of rural voters found that about 75% rated their local cost of living as fair or poor. Nearly half worried about making their rent or mortgage payments. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS The GOP doesn't need another consultant's postmortem to understand what happened. It needs to look at what's happening to the people who feed, build and power this country. Farm production expenses are projected to reach nearly $493 billion in 2026, up 4.5% in a single year, while inflation-adjusted net farm income is expected to fall 5.5%. In 2012, John Deere's flagship combine cost roughly $454,000, when wheat was $7.77 a bushel. Today, its flagship combine costs over $1.1 million, while wheat is projected at $6.91 a bushel. items.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.

items.summary: Illustration by Matt Rota for ProPublica. Animation by Henrike Lendowski for ProPublica. When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top. Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children. Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt. New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. items.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
items.author: Heather Cherone
items.summary: Matt Rota for ProPublica Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess. The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble. The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund. Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole. Sure enough, some of the company’s assets were damaged in the war, although for security reasons it hasn’t disclosed exactly what was hit. Acwa’s net income rose 0.6% in the first nine months of the year compared to the same period last year, but was held back as the war slowed its pipeline of new projects and raised its shipping costs in the region ten-fold. But Serhan remains defiant: “You take the cards you’re dealt and make the best out of it,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Acwa operates nearly 100 gigawatts of gas and renewable power projects in more than a dozen countries, as well as the world’s largest privately held fleet of water desalination plants. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is taking place against the backdrop of a major policy decision: how hard to push to include a spending prohibition on the Iran war in a broader funding bill. Schumer lists the “power of the purse” as an option for curbing the conflict, while Van Hollen is a leading proponent of a funding restriction. items.title: More Americans see DC as safe, poll finds
items.author: Morgan Chalfant
items.summary: More Americans now say Washington, DC, is safe than have said so in 36 years, a statistic that the White House will likely view as a testament to President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown in the nation’s capital. Sixty-four percent of US adults currently view DC as a safe place, according to Gallup, a 12-point increase since 2023. That’s been driven by Republicans: In 2023, 77% of Democrats and only 29% of Republicans said DC was safe; today 70% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans say so. The poll was taken before a recent shooting in DC’s Logan Circle made national headlines. Crime has generally been on the decline in DC, though at least one study found that Trump’s National Guard deployment had minimal effect on violent crime. Another city seeing its highest perceived safety rating since 1990: New York City. — Morgan Chalfant

items.author: Frances Mei Hardin
items.summary: Welcome to Chief Complaint , a new STAT+ column from Frances Mei Hardin, M.D. A former ear, nose, and throat surgeon, she writes about the many challenges facing those who practice medicine in a time of great change. During my second year of residency, my husband drove me to the batting cages for the first time. He’d noticed I was coming home with an increasing level of rage, with nowhere for it to go. I had never swung a bat before, but we spent an hour that evening in a netted room, him slow-pitching and me swinging out of my shoes. My hands stung and my bones shook with every hit, but it was the best that I felt in months. This batting cage salve is about the only type of “physician self-care” that ever actually worked for me, and it didn’t come from a hospital-mandated wellness module, nor a doctor appreciation pizza party. What actually gets prescribed to physicians is basic wellness fare: the mindfulness worksheets, the resilience webinars, the optional yoga in unused office room C in the old hospital annex building. These were some recent affordable housing offerings in the city’s lottery system . But those rents aren’t exactly cheap. You might ask, affordable for whom? In New York City, affordable housing — at least what’s in the housing lottery — is housing where the rent is set at about one-third of household income and receives some sort of government subsidy. The affordable housing in the lottery is rent-stabilized, meaning its price can increase only in increments as approved by the Rent Guidelines Board. items.title: How Our Newsroom Estimated NYC Housing Lottery Odds
items.author: Kennedy Sessions
items.summary: Over the last few months, The City Reporter reviewed data from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development’s Local Law 217 Report , summarizing housing lottery outcomes from Jan. 1, 2022, through Oct. 31, 2024. Our analysis calculated the approximate odds of the more than 10.9 million applications submitted through the city’s Housing Connect portal. The report shows outcomes based on household size, income, and race. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, according to Charter’s AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job. Associates screen his messages, print them out, and respond on his behalf, the Journal reports. The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4% —remains accountable to an independent board. A seismic change has taken hold within her: she will later confide in him of an emotional affair, and a tragic accident that leaves her emotionally unmoored. items.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.author: Ben Aitken
items.summary: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples.

items.author: Tim Warner / Getty
items.summary: In Jules Verne’s wildest imagination, the technology that would send humanity starward was already familiar on Earth. The launching mechanism for the American rocket, in Verne’s 1865 novel From the Earth to the Moon , is—of all things—a colossal cannon. The speed required to reach the lunar surface, he reasoned, would require a gunshot of a launch. So in Vernian terms, a starship was not merely launched but “fired” into space. I’ve been thinking of Verne today as I watched the video (then watched it again, and again) of SpaceX’s latest history-making maneuver. Up until this point, Mechazilla’s chopsticks had caught boosters after launch—that is, the part of the rocket that detaches—but never ships themselves. items.title: Milk and wine used in Menorcan funerary rituals over 2,000 years ago
items.summary: In the Late Iron Age, or post-Talayotic period, over 2,000 years ago, Menorca and the other Balearic Islands experienced increasing connectivity with the wider Mediterranean. However, they also maintained distinctive local funerary traditions, such as burying their loved ones in rock-cut tombs, or artificial caves. Some of these caves contained external courtyards located in front of the burial chambers where animal offerings might have been made. Archaeologists even suspect that perishable foods or liquids were offered in characteristic island containers, such as high-bottomed vessels.

items.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.summary: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights. Read full article Comments

items.title: Common blood pressure drug helps more stroke survivors reach critical health target
items.summary: A low-cost medication could help stroke survivors whose blood pressure remains elevated despite treatment, a new study suggests. The research, known as the REDUCE trial, looked at whether adding spironolactone, a medication commonly known as a water pill, could help lower blood pressure after a stroke. The findings were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions, Nov. 6-9, 2026, in Chicago. Participants were split into two groups. One added spironolactone to their regular treatment, while the other continued with usual post-stroke care . SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE Researchers tracked the participants' blood pressure at home over the following six months to determine whether adding the medication made a difference. After three months, the top blood pressure number was nearly eight points lower on average among people taking spironolactone compared with those receiving usual care – about 126 versus 133, the study said. More patients taking spironolactone also reached the recommended blood pressure goal of less than 130/80. That included 52% of those taking the medication compared with 30% receiving usual care. items.title: What Is a Prop Bet? Player Props, Team Props and Game Props Explained
items.summary: A prop bet is a wager on a specific statistic to happen in the event that doesn’t depend on who wins or loses the game. There are many types of prop markets, and the most common are in football. For example, you could wager on the running back’s rushing yards, or which team (and how) will score score first. Props are some of the most extensive games available in the market and they continue to expand with more options provided on every game. Prop bets are usually how most people build same-game parlays. A prop bet, short for proposition bet, is a wager on a specific outcome inside a game rather than on the final score. The team can lose, and your prop can still win. Sportsbooks post hundreds of props on a single NFL game and dozens on a regular season NBA or MLB game. Props fall into three groups: Most props are either over/under lines on a number or yes/no markets on an event. A few, like first touchdown scorer, list every eligible player at a different price. A prop works like a small bet on a small game. The sportsbook projects a number, sets a line at or near it, and attaches a price to each side. items.title: What Is a Teaser Bet? How Teasers Work in Football and Basketball Betting
items.summary: A teaser bet is when you get to pair two or more plays and adjust the line in one way or another. Bettors use a teaser to give themselves a better price on a play without having to take as big of a risk on covering a spread or total. In exchange for being able to adjust the line, you are paying the book different prices. This will guide you through how to make a teaser bet and what things you should consider before placing the wager. Teasers are offered in football and basketball only, because those are the sports where points scored come in predictable chunks. You will not find a teaser on a baseball or hockey card. A teaser bet is a type of parlay that lets you adjust the point spread or total on every leg by a fixed number of points. In football, the standard teaser is six points. In basketball, it is four. Every leg moves by the same amount and in your favor, and every leg has to win for the ticket to cash. The trade-off is the price. A standard two-team point spread parlay pays about +260. items.title: The experiments improving our understanding of volcanic tsunamis
items.author: Saima May Sidik
items.summary: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves. As a result, it is difficult to anticipate whether a volcanic flow will trigger a tsunami and, if so, how big it will be. Researchers have used laboratory experiments to study this process, but little is known about how well these models mimic reality.

items.title: ‘Silicon Valley’ showrunner on how the HBO comedy predicted today’s tech drama
items.author: Ben Smith
items.summary: The Scene A year before the iconic show debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the show’s creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valley’s power and its eccentricity, but it wasn’t working and he wanted a second opinion. Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he can’t afford. Berg told Judge the scene didn’t make sense: “This is not a guy who’s materialistic,” he said. “He’s an artist.” Berg took over the writer’s room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom — and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release. Cybercriminals are using fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving them access to their Microsoft and Google accounts. And some of these attacks can get past the extra security checks many of us rely on. According to a new report from Push Security, attackers have created convincing event registration pages impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The concerning part is how easily an invitation that appears legitimate can lead to someone handing over access to their work account. Here's what researchers discovered and how to protect yourself. items.title: STAT+: FDA rejects lung cancer treatment ivonescimab from Summit Therapeutics

items.summary: The Food and Drug Administration rejected a treatment for a type of lung cancer developed by the U.S.-based biotech Summit Therapeutics and the Chinese drugmaker Akeso, Summit said on Sunday. In a letter sent to the companies, FDA regulators said the drug, called ivonescimab, could not be approved because it didn’t help patients live longer. While the drug was found to slow lung cancer worsening in patients, the absence of a survival benefit “does not support the positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval,” FDA reviewers concluded. The FDA’s rejection of ivonescimab is a regulatory setback for Summit, which oversees development of the drug outside of China, although one that was not entirely unforeseen. items.summary: Last year, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University revealed startling evidence about the impact of using AI on how—and how hard—people think, finding that among more than 300 knowledge workers, leaning too much on AI tools like ChatGPT was associated with diminished critical thinking skills . The study, mirrored by results from MIT-led research , suggested that even using AI for low-stakes tasks such as proofreading “can lead to significant negative outcomes in high-stakes contexts,” like writing legal documents, the study authors wrote. For the young generation of digital natives navigating AI anxiety around keeping up with peers using the technology and AI displacing them from jobs, the fear of the technology making people dumber is dominant. But that hasn’t stopped them from using AI—even when they’re explicitly told not to. A Wharton-led survey published earlier this year, conducted in partnership with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, found young people are ramping up their AI use, even as their concerns about it causing lazy thinking persist. The finding, published in Scientific Reports, provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.

items.title: Poll: Republicans have a MAGA dilemma after their midterm losses
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.summary: The Republican Party’s midterm wipeout has torn apart President Donald Trump’s coalition. For months, polling has shown cracks among Trump’s 2024 voters over immigration , the Iran war and the president’s influence. Now, new results from The POLITICO Poll , conducted just days after the election, reveal a deep chasm between Trump’s self-identified MAGA base and the non-MAGA voters who helped fuel his return to the White House. The two camps hold sharply different interpretations of the GOP’s historic midterm defeat and what comes next for their party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global. MAGA Trump loyalists were more likely to say the president is not to blame for the losses — that things would have gone better if he was on the ballot — and that the party should now move closer to Trump. Non-MAGA Trump voters starkly disagreed, saying they are ready to move away from him and his unpopular agenda. About one in five said they voted for Democratic candidates this cycle. items.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
items.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

items.title: The Pentagon Ignored a Warning About the Danger of Iran’s Drones
items.author: Arash Khamooshi / Polaris / The New York Times
items.summary: F rom a distance , the Iranian drone resembled an arrowhead, pointing downward as it dove out of the sky. Its propeller, powered by the kind of motor typically used in dirt bikes and lawnmowers, produced a high-pitched wail. It struck midmorning on March 1, the second day of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, hitting a logistics center in Kuwait used by the American military. Dozens of personnel from the Army Reserve were working at an office building there. The incoming drone, a variant of the Shahed, slammed through the roof of the building and detonated its payload. Six American service members were killed and more than two dozen wounded, several of them critically—the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war. It will be hard for the survivors to forget the drone’s distinctive noise. In Ukraine, which has faced years of attacks from this type of drone, people often compare its sound as it falls out of the sky to a Vespa revving its engine. But the noise no longer terrifies Ukrainians the way it once did. Last year, Ukraine’s arms industry developed a cheap and effective way to shoot down Shaheds. The U.S. military knew about this technology months before the war in Iran began.

items.title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington
items.author: Emma Beddington
items.summary: People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated? I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies , on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”. Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders?

I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.

items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.author: Shadi Khan Saif
items.summary: For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “ Tawakkul ba Khuda, ” he replied. He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.

items.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
items.author: Tim Dowling
items.summary: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”

items.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stranded, dressed as a flapper, on a freezing night. Then a cheerful taxi driver pulled over
items.author: Carole Edmunds as told to Katie Cunningham
items.summary: My tyre was blown so he changed it for me. When I offered payment, he said ‘Don’t be ridiculous love’ Read more in the kindness of strangers series I had to fight not to lose control of the car. I was in my early 20s and driving home from a fancy dress party when bang – my tyre suddenly blew. I managed to wrestle my Toyota Corolla to a stop without crashing and sat there, heart pounding, as I wondered what to do next. It was 1982 in Canberra; a foggy, bitterly cold night in the middle of winter. I was wearing a silly flapper dress and high heels – I’m not sure I’d even packed a jacket! I had a spare tyre in the back, but little idea how to change it. My options were to make the one hour walk home alone or wait to see if another car passed and could offer me a ride. For 30 minutes I sat in the driver’s seat helplessly, unsure what to do.

items.title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
items.author: Emily Foxhall, The Texas Tribune
items.summary: On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state . It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology , while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster. The Texas Railroad Commission , which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this Exxon Mobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision. The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working-class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe. items.title: Could brain energy mismatches explain altered experiences in schizophrenia?
items.author: Sanjukta Mondal
items.summary: A minute can seem shorter when you are having fun, yet it feels painfully long when you're bored or stressed. Although this gap between actual time and perceived time is something we all experience, it can be much more pronounced in people with schizophrenia-spectrum conditions. They may experience time and space very differently from others, with time seeming fragmented, familiar surroundings feeling strange or disconnected, and even their sense of self shifting.

items.title: New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
items.author: Shreejaya Karantha
items.summary: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.

items.title: From the Lost Generation to Gen Beta: How every generation got its name
items.author: Steven John
items.summary: Generation Beta had a name before its first members were born. The label for babies born from 2025 through 2039 was already in headlines in late 2024, courtesy of the Australian demographer who also named the generation before it, Gen Alpha . That is a long way from how this used to work. The Lost Generation got its name secondhand, from a French garage owner, via Gertrude Stein and Ernest Hemingway. A network news anchor named the Greatest Generation more than half a century after it went to war. There’s no official process for naming a generation; it’s more like a cultural quorum is reached, and a name takes hold, even though it’s never technically fixed. The moniker for tens of millions of people born within a couple of decades of one another can come from a magazine essay, a novel, or a research firm. The only real key to a name sticking is that lots of people start using it. The labels carry real money. McCrindle, the research firm behind Gen Alpha, projects that cohort will command $5.46 trillion in spending power by 2029 .
