items.summary: A few weeks ago, a chatbot read a tranche of my text messages spanning more than a dozen years and declared that I’d been a bad friend. First, some context: I’m writing a memoir about my love life, or lack thereof, so I’ve been going through old correspondence and quizzing friends about their memories of the years when I was single (2012–22) and not so single (2022–now). One of those friends is Michael—who, like me, is unmarried; who, like me, has an extensive history of encounters facilitated by dating apps; and who, like me, was long looking for love but often found himself disappointed. My text history with Michael goes back to 2014, when we first met. Sometimes, we’re in touch daily. At other times, we go weeks, months, even a year without communicating (for reasons that have never been entirely clear to us). Six years ago, I moved from New York, where Michael lives, to Los Angeles, so since then, our friendship has been conducted largely via phone. This means that an already rich history of friendship has become richer, not just because of the accumulation of our shared experiences, but also because of the way our communications have been automatically documented and archived.

items.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.author: Melissa Denes
items.summary: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

items.title: Nonprofit celebrates return of program that sends free books to Wisconsin prisoners
items.author: Sarah Lehr / WPR
items.summary: Reading Time: 2 minutes A nonprofit group is once again sending free books to prisoners across the state. Since 2006, Wisconsin Books to Prisoners has mailed roughly 70,000 books to Wisconsin inmates, who wrote to the group requesting specific titles or topics. But, in 2024, Wisconsin’s Department of Corrections told Books to Prisoners it could no longer send used books. That prompted the volunteer-led group to curtail its operations — leading to devastating consequences for the people locked up in state prisons, said Wisconsin Books to Prisoners co-founder Camy Matthay. “Our project was extremely critical to prisoners who wanted to read books that were more current and relevant to their ambitions,” Matthay said. Over the last two years, Books to Prisoners has been working with the Department of Corrections to find a solution. That included pilot programs, which tested out book shipments to specific prisons. As of this month, Books to Prisoners is back to sending new and gently used books to all of Wisconsin’s state prisons. items.author: Russell Contreras
items.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. items.summary: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . items.summary: I f you are looking for government corruption, Washington has always been a target-rich environment. But the past two years of the Trump administration have seen the swamp rise to extraordinary levels. Despite remarkable threats from the White House suggesting that congressional investigations might be a crime , Democrats are preparing to scrutinize what Senator Raphael Warnock has called “the most corrupt administration in American history.” Many Democrats will be tempted to go directly after the president for his misdeeds. A better strategy would be to take a page from the prosecutor’s playbook on investigating organized crime. In many ways Trump and his inner circle resemble an organized crime family, with Donald as the don. Such groups are tightly knit, held together by bonds of unwavering loyalty to the organization and its authoritarian leader. They prize secrecy. They enforce their demands through intimidation and coercion. The members work to enrich themselves, displaying little regard for law or institutions. items.summary: New exhibition restores painter’s place as leading figure in French movement that revolutionised art As a painter, friend, and collaborator of Edgar Degas, who exhibited with impressionist artists including Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, Mary Cassatt was at the heart of the 19th-century movement that emerged in France and revolutionised art. items.title: Brazil’s fertilizer gap is a global food risk
items.author: Lorenzo Rosa
items.summary: Brazilian agriculture feeds roughly 800 million people , about 10% of the world’s population. In 2024, according to World Trade Organization data , Brazil exported US$144.4 billion in agricultural products while importing just US$15.4 billion — a net surplus of roughly US$129 billion, more than four times Argentina’s, the next-largest net agricultural exporter. Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of soybeans, beef, poultry, coffee, sugar and orange juice , and a top-three producer and exporter of corn . Brazil alone supplies more than half of global soybean trade . The world’s food supply increasingly depends on Brazil, and Brazil’s harvests depend on fertilizer it barely produces. That is the paradox: the country that feeds so much of the world cannot feed its own fields without imports from a handful of foreign suppliers. Its farms run on three nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — and, according to the latest UN Food and Agriculture Organization data, in 2024, Brazil imports roughly 90% of the fertilizer it used. items.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital. When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. items.title: Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
items.author: Neel Dhanesha
items.summary: An angler displays a lake trout, considered an invasive species, that they caught on Lake McDonald in Glacier National Park in Montana on October 18, 2023. | Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana. We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison. The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way. The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations , and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses . What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. items.summary: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care.

items.title: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’

items.summary: As a lone female traveller, the prospect of staying in a hut on Rannoch Moor is daunting, but the silence of the mountains and lochs turns out to be ‘the ultimate luxury’ In the gloaming, the trees stand dark and impenetrable on either side of the path. An owl, wide-faced and pale as a spectre, glides out of the pines ahead of me. Heart pounding, I pick up speed and continue uphill, the silence thick around me. Just a few minutes earlier, I had been scuffing my feet in the sand by the loch shore, watching as the clouds draped themselves across the top of the Grampians. In the absence of other people, Loch Laidon, silvery in the half-light, had been mine to enjoy; in the woods, however, my solitude feels unnerving.

Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé . We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience. A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. items.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
items.summary: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

items.title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers

The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

items.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
items.summary: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

items.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
items.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

items.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.summary: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

PAHO had planned to announce the determination publicly on Tuesday, Nov. 17, according to KFF Health News, which separately reported the decision, citing researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations. WISCONSIN INFANT DIES OF MEASLES AS STATE SEES FIRST DEATH FROM DISEASE SINCE 1990 The country has held elimination status since 2000. Isolated cases and shorter outbreaks can still occur without forfeiting that status. PAHO’s independent regional verification commission reviewed countries’ elimination status during its Nov. 10-13 meeting in Washington, D.C. The U.S. reported 5,412 confirmed measles cases in 2026 through Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The then– Nvidia CEO had a gospel to share with the politicians, tech executives, and journalists, Fortune among them, crowding the room: The AI boom was only getting started, and Nvidia was in town to help bankroll it. “I’m gonna invest in you! I’m gonna invest in you!” he shouted at the founders in the crowd. “We’re not your largest investor, but we are your best investor.” Huang’s London visit was one stop on a European charm offensive that also swept through France, Sweden, and Germany. At the time, the trip had the feeling of a victory lap. Nvidia is the default supplier of the vital chips that are fueling the AI industry’s rapid growth, and with a market cap that, at one point, topped $5.7 trillion, had seeded an entire ecosystem that came to depend on Nvidia’s support. If the AI boom is a kind of religion, then Huang had been its high priest—proselytizing to investors and policymakers, ministering to the faithful, and doling out alms to needy startups, AI labs, and neoclouds. items.title: The Ceaseless Ceasefire
items.author: Safia Southey
items.summary: All across the world, people are trapped by forces far beyond their control. Handcuffed by situations which they are powerless to change. I spent countless hours talking to people like this from Southeast Asia to North Africa. Their immediate circumstances couldn’t have been more different. They hailed from radically dissimilar backgrounds; they were of different races, ethnicities, and religions. But they were bound together by one unifying force: organized, armed violence. Or, rather, the imposition of it upon them. These people were just living their lives when war arrived on their doorsteps. When most people think of war, they think of armed soldiers. But I think of grandmothers and toddlers. Modern war zones are much more the province of civilians than combatants, even if the traditional “battlefield” has made a significant reappearance this century. Soldiers die. Civilians die in droves. Soldiers deploy here and there. Civilians are put to flight, en masse, often again and again. items.title: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
items.author: Amy Maxmen / KFF Health News
items.summary: Reading Time: 8 minutes The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago. Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States. “It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.” Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread. items.title: A single CRISPR infusion lowers blood fats in monkeys for three years

items.summary: High levels of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which are types of blood fats, are major contributors to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Gene-editing technologies offer a potential alternative to lipid-lowering medications. In a new CRISPR experiment, a single infusion of a gene-editing treatment kept triglyceride levels low in monkeys for three years. The findings support the possibility of controlling blood fats with a lasting DNA change, potentially replacing daily doses of medication.

items.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
items.author: Donica Phifer
items.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S. The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop. Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said. Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday. items.author: Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
items.summary: Measles is undeniably back. The disease, which was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, is once again endemic, the Pan American Health Organization reportedly decided at a meeting this week. PAHO made that determination based on a set of technical standards, and its official declaration is expected early next week. Those criteria say that measles is endemic when the same strain of the virus causes continuous infections for a year straight; even before this week’s meeting, publicly available data indicated that this was likely the case. But really, the evidence has been clear for some time now: The U.S. is in the midst of a measles crisis unlike any it’s faced in decades. More than 5,000 cases in 45 states have been confirmed this year. Pennsylvania started reporting measles deaths this August; its count is now up to seven. New York has had one death. Wisconsin reported its second yesterday. This is already America’s worst year for measles since 1991, which marked the end of a three-year epidemic in which 123 people died. But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

items.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
items.author: Jacek Krywko
items.summary: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. items.title: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis
items.summary: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

items.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

items.summary: The first ever Eurovision Asia song contest takes place in Thailand on Saturday, and it won’t disappoint those hoping for some bizarre acts The first ever Eurovision Asia is being held in Thailand on Saturday. The event is a more compact affair than the European version has become, and with only 11 countries competing, it isn’t a straightforward cultural import. None of the entrants have gone near wacky Eurovision vibes such as having a singing turkey or banana-eating wolves . Restrictive attitudes to homosexuality in some of the countries where the show will be broadcast have also tempered the overt campness and LGBTQ+ representation with which Eurovision has come to be associated – there will certainly not be an equivalent of Olly Alexander getting sweaty in a grubby gym changing room .

items.title: When Walmart pulls out of town, the stores next door don’t pick up its shoppers — their sales are down 20% a year later
items.author: Vivek Astvansh, Preetinder Kaur, Pushpinder Gill, The Conversation
items.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map

items.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
items.author: Courtenay Brown
items.summary: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves. Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up. Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month. These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers. Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines. Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California. The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food. A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices. items.summary: I n the spring of 1943, Walter C. Langer, a psychoanalyst at Harvard, received a query from William J. Donovan, the head of the U.S. government’s Office of Strategic Services, the covert-operations predecessor to the CIA. Donovan was interested in commissioning Langer to prepare a psychological profile of Adolf Hitler. “What we need is a realistic appraisal of the German situation,” Donovan told Langer. “If Hitler is running the show, what kind of a person is he? What are his ambitions? How does he appear to the German people? What is he like with his associates?” The OSS chief wanted to understand Hitler’s “psychological make-up—the things that make him tick.” Donovan was especially keen to know how Hitler might respond to increasing adversity. Hitler was used to winning. From 1933 to 1943, the Nazi leader had marched from one stunning political and military triumph to the next, securing the chancellorship, crushing the German constitutional order, annexing Austria, dismembering Czechoslovakia, and then invading Poland, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, countries across North Africa, and Russia. items.title: What the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Means to Its Guards
items.author: Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic. Sources: John Greim / LightRocket / Ge
items.summary: I n the autumn of 1921 , the U.S. Army faced a difficult choice. Among four identical, flag-draped caskets—each containing the unidentified remains of an American soldier killed in World War I—only one would be laid to rest at the new Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery. It seemed only appropriate that an experienced commissioned officer ought to make the selection. All four men had died in the war and been buried at American cemeteries in France. But when word came that the French military had asked an enlisted man to pick France’s Unknown Soldier, the Americans quickly determined that they would not be one-upped by French egalitarianism on that day. That is how the selection came to be made by Edward Younger, a 23-year-old sergeant and one of the pallbearers who had carried the four caskets under consideration. Younger had survived being knocked unconscious by a shell and later being shot through the left thigh during vicious fighting in World War I. Police departments struggled to receive online crime reports, hospitals fell back on other ways to communicate, and some government services were suspended. The disruption exposed how deeply governments and essential public services now depend on a single private company’s technology, and how something as ordinary as an email outage can interfere with the systems people rely on for public safety, health care, and justice. Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season. Americans, it turns out, aren’t nearly as eager to hand over their gift lists. Nearly three-quarters of Americans, or 72%, say they don’t plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025, according to a new Bank of America survey . The 23-percentage-point jump suggests a gap between the industry’s ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it. The reasons shoppers gave suggest that when it comes to gifts, efficiency isn’t the point. Among those who don’t plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they don’t trust AI recommendations. items.summary: In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of GPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites. The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.” At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. In the absence of solid information from trusted authorities, people interpret crises through the prism of their preexisting concerns. A safety planner’s job is to envision the full range of possible threats and assess how likely each one is to occur. items.title: How to Land 4,000 Planes During a Ground Stop
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Source: FlightAware.
items.summary: For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out. Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” some 4,000 airplanes were in the sky, headed for U.S. airports, according to Flightradar24, an aviation-tracking website. Even if no more flights took off, all of those planes needed to land. For the people below, getting them down safely became an immediate preoccupation. This type of nationwide grounding had happened only twice before in recent history—once after the September 11 attacks, and once in January 2023 for about an hour and a half. Every aircraft still aloft needed to make it to its destination, despite apparently spotty communications. Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. Known as long-range reconnaissance patrols, or LRRPs, these small teams of six to eight soldiers were dropped behind enemy lines to track supply routes and hostile positions, sometimes for days at a time. items.title: America’s AI secrets are leaking — and not just because of the Nvidia spy scandal
items.author: Sigal Samuel
items.summary: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images TORONTO — When a company is building technology that could totally transform the world — technology so high-stakes and secretive that it may underpin the future of geopolitics — you might expect its leaders to have a handle on the basics of security. Basics like, say, not having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Basics like not selling the tech to someone who may help smuggle it to a top foreign adversary. Instead America got Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned Thursday after admitting that he’d had just such an affair. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. items.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
items.author: Jacek Krywko
items.summary: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). items.title: GLP-1s often contain untested additive combinations, study finds
items.author: Sophia Friesen
items.summary: Use of GLP-1 receptor agonist medications (GLP-1s) has skyrocketed in recent years, and many people are using "compounded" GLP-1 products: medicines that include GLP-1s as well as other active substances, some of which are not regulated by the FDA. A new study found that compounded GLP-1s now make up a large majority of weight-loss medicines, commonly containing vitamin B12 analogs that have not been tested for safety in combination with GLP-1s.

items.title: Personalized therapies for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis may follow from method that identifies harmful gut bacteria
items.summary: Which gut bacteria contribute to the development or worsening of chronic inflammation? An international research team led by Dr. Lukas Mager from University Hospital Tübingen and Prof. Kathy McCoy from the University of Calgary has developed an approach to identify and selectively target such bacteria. The researchers identified two bacterial species that promote intestinal inflammation and compounds that selectively inhibit their growth. Published in the journal Gut, the study could pave the way for personalized therapies for inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

items.title: A perfect couple: Chromium keeps ruthenium grounded in water electrolysis

Yet, these differences make them perfect for each other. According to researchers at ICFO, chemical interactions between atoms are not that different. Ruthenium, for instance, belongs to the "dreamer" class. It is commonly used in single-atom catalysts that speed up water electrolysis, which splits water to obtain green hydrogen.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current. "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote. Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader. Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job. The House voted 211-204 this week to divert an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Hegseth. House Republicans moved to block a straight, up-or-down vote on impeachment. items.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.summary: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

items.summary: Next time you ask AI for medical advice, you may want to consider whether it’s been influenced by Big Pharma. The study authors conducted experiments with a dozen consumer-facing large language models (LLMs), including versions of Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT—made by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, respectively. Clinical guidance or commercial influence? The models were tested across 33 scenarios that each included a clinical case description and multiple treatment options. In some cases, the AI models were also given an ad for one of the treatment options. The ad’s content included information about the drug and its uses, but did not specifically direct the AI model to recommend the drug. When exposed to an ad, AI models recommended the treatment in question an average of 47.6% of the time, compared with 35% when no ad was present. However, the size of these shifts varied among the 12 models. When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges. Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle . A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. (Although Scots survives as a minority language with many regional variations, none of them closely resemble MacDiarmid’s concoction.) I loved the verse for its woozy lyricism and nerded out on the text’s annotations; I was also fascinated by the author’s grand ambitions. MacDiarmid was part of a cultural movement known as the Scottish Renaissance, whose writers sought to revive the once-independent nation’s dialects and traditions. But did he really think he could kick off a national resurgence by inventing a language no reader could easily understand? And what would drive a writer to even try? items.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said .

In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October , resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month. Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.

items.author: Neil Irwin
items.summary: A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system . The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000. A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults haven’t made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm. Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generation’s stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election. The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young people’s relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job — but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap). For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. items.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.summary: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. items.title: GLP-1 drugs taken by 30 million Americans now carry an FDA warning for a rare ‘stroke of the eye’ that can cause vision loss

items.summary: GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye. I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION . Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions . The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so. items.author: Charlie Hunt, The Conversation
items.summary: During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia . Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians. There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand. By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander .” So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House? items.title: Friday the 13th is here. Its impact on your work day may not be so scary
items.author: Shannon Cudd
items.summary: Business can be risky, so it’s natural that superstitions can sometimes creep in when money and careers are at stake. This workweek ends on Friday the 13th, so in the Western world, the stage is set for fear to influence commerce. Let’s take a look at the so-called bad luck day’s origins and how it impacts the business world. What is a fear of Friday the 13th called? A fear of Friday the 13th is called “paraskevidekatriaphobia,” a term created by psychotherapist Donald Dossey . It combines the Greek words for Friday, 13, and fear. How many Friday the 13ths are there in a year? Around every 212.35 days, a Friday the 13th occurs. This figure is based on a complete 400-year Gregorian calendar cycle. Another way to look at it: there is at least one Friday the 13th a year, but there can be up to three. This year, 2026, Friday the 13th will be in triplicate. When did Friday the 13th become unlucky? The truth is, no one really knows how exactly Friday the 13th became synonymous with misfortune. There are historical and religious references that might shed some light. items.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.summary: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. items.title: Climate Advisers director: The U.S. needs a clean energy standard for AI data centers
items.author: Matt Piotrowski
items.summary: Voters delivered a verdict on data centers in the midterm election. In an NBC News exit poll, 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and voters passed more than 40 local measures restricting data centers. Lawmakers now face a choice. They can answer with bans, or with rules that decide who pays for AI’s power but ignore where it comes from. Either would be half a policy. Voters want lower bills and cleaner air, and clean energy can address both. Ireland, Singapore and China have already tied data center growth to clean power. The United States should too. Residents outside Memphis have seen the alternative. xAI has run dozens of gas turbines across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, drawing lawsuits and complaints over air quality . More are coming. Global Energy Monitor counts 189 GW of natural gas tied to data centers in development as of mid-2026, with about 17 GW already under construction . items.title: Democrats won Congress. Now they must win back trade policy

Some in the party are focusing on reining in Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on allies like Canada, while others hope that a 2029 Democratic President might direct Trump’s expansive tariffs toward progressive priorities, such as raising labor standards. This debate is missing two things. First, it blames trade failures on Trump, when both the Trump and Biden administrations pursued similar trade policies that failed workers. Second, it focuses on taking tariff power back from the president but overlooks Congress’s role in setting trade objectives. I have spent my career trying to make trade work for American workers. As a progressive, I urge congressional Democrats to take stock of the lessons from both the Trump and Biden administrations, which requires a course correction, even if it means restraining a future Democratic president. items.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
items.author: Bob Berwyn, Inside Climate News
items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus. Read full article Comments

She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. items.title: DR Congo president enacts referendum law

items.summary: DR Congo’s president has signed a law allowing the constitution to be changed or replaced through a referendum, a move opponents warn could pave the way for him to seek a third term in the mineral-rich country. Félix Tshisekedi, in power since 2019, is due to complete his second and final term under the current constitution in just over two years. He said in May he was not seeking constitutional changes to stay in power, but would accept a third term if the Congolese people wanted it. The country was ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko for three decades until his overthrow in 1997. After years of war, its 2006 constitution introduced safeguards against a return to dictatorship, including presidential term limits. But Tshisekedi’s predecessor, Joseph Kabila, still stayed in office for two years after his final term expired. Opposition leaders have joined forces to resist any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s rule, organizing protests at home and seeking support from European governments. They argue that a referendum cannot override the constitution’s ban on changing presidential term limits. — Ruben Nyanguila

items.title: Ghana sets out $10B investment plan
items.author: Ruben Nyanguila
items.summary: Ghana aims to invest $10 billion over four years to expand domestic production and reduce its dependence on raw commodity exports, as the West African country seeks to turn its recovery from a debt crisis into employment growth and higher incomes. Presenting the budget, the finance minister told lawmakers “too little value” was added domestically. As part of the push to shift the economy, Africa’s largest gold producer wants to phase out exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030. Much of the skilled employment linked to its mineral wealth currently takes place abroad, the finance ministry says. The government is targeting economic growth of 8% by 2030 and the budget has allocated $2.6 billion to support agriculture, energy, and manufacturing over the next year. Ghana completed an IMF bailout program this year and now plans to repay about $3 billion in domestic and international debt ahead of schedule. — Ruben Nyanguila

items.title: Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive
items.author: Reed Albergotti
items.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow. The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled “Stand with Jensen,” and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company. The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him . Notable Several names have been floated for who could replace Huang, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, or even, on President Donald Trump’s suggestion , former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

items.title: STAT+: Senators introduce bill to curb conflicts of interest on preventive care panel
items.author: Chelsea Cirruzzo
items.summary: WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services. The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest. The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: The Democrats Who Are Stunned to Find Themselves in Congress
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic*
items.summary: Z ack Mullock spent the past nine months campaigning for a U.S. House seat, but never actually pictured himself in Washington as a newly elected member of Congress. Yes, the mayor of Cape May, on the southern tip of New Jersey, believed in his long-shot congressional campaign. But the Democrat never really stopped to think about what would happen if he won. And why would he have? As of late October, political prognosticators still rated the seat he was running for, New Jersey’s Second Congressional District, as safely Republican. After Mullock eked out a shock victory against Representative Jeff Van Drew on November 3, there was a lot to do. For one thing, he had to Google how much members of Congress make ($174,000 a year—more than 10 times what he was paid to serve as mayor). Mullock, a 41-year-old father of three, also had to scramble his travel plans. He had scheduled a vacation for immediately after the election to mark the end of an exhausting stretch for his family. Then someone informed him that he needed to show up at freshman orientation instead. “The first thing I had to tell my kids was, ‘We’re not going to Florida, guys. I’m sorry,’” Mullock told us. items.title: Baldwin Group CEO: The biggest AI disruption in insurance is the advisor
items.author: Trevor Baldwin
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is going to disrupt insurance brokerage. There is not much question about that. The question that matters is what gets disrupted, and how differently firms are preparing for it. Most firms are approaching AI the way they approached every prior wave of technology: take the work as it exists and do it faster. But AI is dramatically changing the economics of gathering information, comparing coverage and facilitating transactions. A firm whose value lives in those activities is competing in a race to the bottom. A firm built on specialized expertise, deep client relationships and experiential human judgment can change the paradigm, turning risk into opportunity for clients. Firms that make that leap go from being a vendor of downside protection to a business partner that helps a client achieve the fullness of their ambition. Their value becomes constrained only by what their clients can achieve. Showing up that way requires the fortitude to completely rebuild how the work gets done. items.title: This Ford sculptor has carved cars out of clay for 40 years. AI and VR just cut his work time in half
items.author: Nick Lichtenberg
items.summary: John “Rex” Allen is 68, wears cowboy boots, a black baseball cap, and he’s spent four decades building life-size cars out of clay. These days he builds inside a virtual-reality headset, too. He does his work upstairs at Ford Motor Company’s gleaming new headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, where the bird sounds in the yard aren’t even real. Just over four miles away, the 109-year-old Rouge Plant looks much the way it did in the 1920s, except with 3D-printed parts patching the factory together and a “Green Roof” overhead that is one of the world’s largest. The green roof at the Ford Rouge Plant. The mobilization was eventually canceled before I deployed, but, by that time, Matt was already being mic’ed up to get onstage. I have thought about that week every day since, and I have come to believe the orders were the most honest test a CEO can face: proof, on a date I did not choose, of whether I had built a durable company or a team that could not function without me. But it’s time to start looking at the Rust Belt city as a warning about the future. As the artificial intelligence revolution unfolds, debates about its impact on the American economy often hinge on the belief that if the technology creates more jobs than it destroys, it will be a success. But the more important question is often the most overlooked: Who will bear the costs of the AI revolution? Youngstown is a symbol for what can happen when America stands idly by as market forces inflict abrupt economic transition on communities. And the next Youngstown may already be taking shape. It may not depend on a steel mill, but on concentrations of jobs increasingly vulnerable to AI. From Huntsville, Texas, to State College, Pennsylvania, the industries will be different, but the risk is familiar: jobs transformed or eliminated faster than the community around them can adapt. items.title: Why BMI Is Not the Best Measure of Health

For years, however, doctors have found that BMI isn’t the best measure of obesity-related health, since it can’t distinguish between fat and muscle weight. items.title: Democrats in power confront the social media trap
items.author: Jim VandeHei
items.summary: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both cautious, calm, compromise-minded leaders fantasizing about a serious, sensible Democratic-run Congress. But social media is a temptress no party leader has tamed. The seduction of attention, likes and followers invariably proves too strong for the savviest, most self-promotional politicians to resist. Why it matters: That's the lesson of the Internet Era of American Politics — the algorithms always win. A few provocative members of Congress and online activists dominate the national conversation because they master the biggest social media platforms. Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software. There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight. The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong. Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended. The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states. Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. items.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
items.author: Ben Berke
items.summary: The Vineyard Wind farm off the coast of Massachusetts in May Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts. Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea. He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast. Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke. The company never came. Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Then-President Joe Biden gave a speech at Brayton Point in Somerset, Massachusetts, in 2022. Four years later, the promised factory has been canceled. items.author: Charisma Madarang
items.summary: Mike McCready rolled out his latest track "Farewell to Seasons" on Friday, the title track from his upcoming "lost" rock opera.

items.author: Andy Greene
items.summary: With the Rolling Stones on hiatus, guitarist Ron Wood has kept himself busy with a solo tour that's coming to New York's Beacon Theater on March 22.
