items.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.

items.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
items.summary: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

items.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
items.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

items.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
items.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.

items.title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
items.summary: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

items.title: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
items.summary: A major study of nearly 1,900 older adults suggests that stopping statins after age 70 may be relatively safe in the short term for people who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke. However, a higher rate of serious cardiovascular events or death during longer follow-up raises questions about the risks of discontinuing these widely prescribed medications.

items.title: Chip curbs may have long-term negative impacts on AI
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: A growing consensus in Washington towards tightening restrictions on China’s access to cutting-edge chip technology will have a negative, long-term impact on the AI sector and the US itself, a leading outlet warned. New regulations and legislation aiming in particular to cut off “remote access” — whereby Chinese firms use US-made processors via data centers in third countries — “ will have consequences ,” SemiAnalysis warned, “and we don’t think politicians are thinking them through.” Today’s status quo offers Washington insight into the activities of Chinese AI firms, leverage to cut off remote access, and has dulled Beijing’s motivations to speedily develop its own chip sector. “Maybe biggest of all,” because Chinese labs largely develop open-source AI, “open source is under attack.” — Prashant Rao

items.title: Commonwealth Fusion’s CEO sees UAE primed for new energy tech
items.author: Mohammed Sergie
items.summary: The Scene When Massachusetts-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems looked for companies that could produce large metal components and complex machinery for its prototype, it landed on the oil and gas industry. CEO Bob Mumgaard said the hydrocarbons industry shares many of the same skills and tools that fusion developers need to achieve a breakthrough and eventually take a share of the energy mix. The UAE is well positioned to use its expertise in oil and gas to adopt fusion technology, Mumgaard said, especially after it has developed a track record of building nuclear power plants and its embrace of AI. “They understand what energy leadership and first mover advantage, advanced technologies can bring to their society, their place in the world,” he said. Abu Dhabi’s government-owned fusion fund, Plynth Energy, acquired a minority stake worth more than $100 million in Commonwealth this year, according to Axios. The US company raised $1 billion in July, bringing its total funding to $4 billion, which Mumgaard said would be enough to build the prototype and prepare for a larger, utility-scale plant in the early 2030s. Next decade Scientists have long predicted that the fusion breakthrough

items.title: EU AI summit expected to be overshadowed by Ukraine war
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: European leaders were set to hold talks on how to compete with the US and China in the AI race, but analysts voiced skepticism the EU could overcome structural shortcomings. The summit in Dublin, the first of its kind to focus solely on AI, is expected to be overshadowed by debate over financial support for Ukraine, discussion over who speaks for the bloc internationally, and horse-trading over an EU-wide budget. The EU’s efforts on AI have in any case so far been scattershot and largely fallen shy of their stated targets . Europe is “a large economy but clearly far behind the US and China,” one leading analyst noted recently, “ which is why it has no seat at the table .” — Prashant Rao

items.title: FTC to block $3.5B veterinary merger
items.author: Rohan Goswami
items.summary: The Scoop The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again. The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival. The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said. Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment. Rohan’s view Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission — even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested. It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trump’s agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires. The FTC is also plan

items.title: Gaming industry poll finds most Americans see prediction markets as gambling
items.author: Eleanor Mueller
items.summary: A bipartisan 82% majority of Americans think that prediction markets should be regulated as gambling products instead of financial ones, a poll conducted by Qualtrics on behalf of the American Gaming Association found. The poll also found that 75% say using the markets to buy and sell sports-related event contracts is the same as using a sportsbook to bet on sports. The group is using the findings, shared first with Semafor , to reinforce its argument that states and tribes should oversee the markets instead of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ahead of a looming Supreme Court ruling . “In an era of political division, Americans are overwhelmingly united against Kalshi’s deceptive marketing of sports gambling as investing,” AGA President and CEO Bill Miller said.

items.title: Demand remains strong for Anthropic IPO despite tech pullback
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is reportedly six times oversubscribed , reflecting bullishness on the AI trade despite recent headwinds. Fears of overspending and soaring debt piles have led investors to pull out from tech stocks in recent weeks, with the Nasdaq index registering its biggest monthly loss in over a year in October. The resignation of the CEO of Nvidia, a firm that has underpinned much of the global AI buildout, has amplified concerns. However, some investors appear undaunted, likely owing to upbeat predictions for future growth: Goldman Sachs, one of the banks leading Anthropic’s IPO, said it expected the firm’s revenue to exceed $600 billion by 2030, more than 130 times its sales last year. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: Nigeria election body to comply with presidential candidate ruling
items.author: Alexis Akwagyiram
items.summary: The News Nigeria’s electoral commission will obey any court ruling on whether the main challenger to President Bola Tinubu is eligible to contest January’s presidential election, its chairman said, potentially handing the judiciary a key role in Africa’s biggest poll. Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is set to appeal last week’s high court ruling that invalidated his candidacy . The chair of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Joash Amupitan, speaking at the Chatham House think tank in London, said the body would be constitutionally “obligated” to “obey every court order” if the appeal fails. INEC’s position adds to uncertainty around the vote in Africa’s top crude oil producer with less than 10 weeks until polls open.The commission is currently embroiled in more than 300 legal cases related to local elections, Amupitan said, adding that unresolved disputes could complicate its preparations for the forthcoming polls. Credibility test Bukola Idowa, executive director of civil society group Kimpact Development Initiative, warned any impression that the electoral process was opaque would undermine the validity of the vote. “We’re looking at an election that will put the

items.title: South Africa’s Ramaphosa takes AI pitch to Musk's turf
items.author: Tiisetso Motsoeneng
items.summary: The News South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment. The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as “openly racist” and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africa’s biggest economy. The working visit , which kicks off on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World summit , unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program. US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africa’s mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Afric

items.title: US commerce secretary in the spotlight over Nvidia scandal
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced mounting pressure from lawmakers over the Trump administration’s handling of the Nvidia scandal. Lutnick has been criticized — including, reportedly, by the Treasury secretary — over his department’s failure to sanction Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, for allegedly smuggling its chips; revelations that a Megaspeed executive, who is accused of ties to Chinese intelligence, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang led to Huang’s downfall. Singapore authorities, meanwhile, said the US provided only “limited” help with the city-state’s investigation into the Megaspeed executive. Multiple Republican senators have called for Lutnick and Huang to appear before the chamber over the still-unfurling episode, while a Republican member of the House told Semafor “ questions need to be answered .” — Prashant Rao

items.title: Trump threatens new tariffs on Mexican goods
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: US President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it doesn’t stop a migrant caravan heading for the border, ratcheting up tensions with the US’ biggest trading partner. Illegal crossings of the US-Mexico border have plummeted during Trump’s second term partly because Mexico, which sends the vast majority of its exports to its northern neighbor, has deployed troops to stem the flow and win over the White House. The Democratic Party’s recent electoral victories have lifted hopes of a warmer US welcome among would-be migrants. However, Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller — the architect of Washington’s draconian approach to immigration, including divisive raids — to become the president’s chief of staff has dashed hopes of a friendlier policy any time soon. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: Opinion: STAT+: ‘What will I do with the time I have left?’: What it’s like to find out you might develop Alzheimer’s
items.author: Jason Karlawish
items.summary: This is the second of two pieces about the experiencing of pre-clinical Alzheimer’s. Read the first here . In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “ The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease ” with this notably qualified call to action: “In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.” Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: The future of heart drug research in the wake of study setbacks
items.author: Adam Feuerstein and Elaine Chen
items.summary: On this week’s episode of “The Readout LOUD”: the failure of two closely followed heart disease drugs and how these setbacks may impact the future of cardiovascular drug research. Plus, drug safety concerns weigh on some of the biggest companies in the sector. For years, it was widely believed that a deeper understanding of genetics was going to speed the development of newer and better medicines for patients with heart disease. But then came this year’s American Heart Association meeting, which was dominated by presentations of clinical trials that showed no benefit whatsoever for two drugs long thought to be genetically validated. Read the rest...

items.title: 5 takeaways from STAT’s investigation of the sprawling ‘three-parent IVF’ industry
items.author: Megan Molteni
items.summary: The investigation started with a tip from a British couple. After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “ three-parent IVF ,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person. Read the rest...

items.title: STAT+: Oura’s acquisition of health tech startup raises conflict-of-interest questions for Eli Lilly, experts say
items.author: Elaine Chen
items.summary: Pharma companies that make GLP-1 drugs have increasingly promoted telehealth companies that prescribe the popular treatments. With a new deal announced this week, one of those relationships is expected to grow more complicated. Eli Lilly has been featuring a telehealth company called Counsel Health on a list of providers for patients seeking a GLP-1 prescription. On Tuesday, Counsel said it would be acquired by the smart ring maker Oura , allowing Counsel clinicians access to the data gathered through the ring so they can help customers understand the data and then diagnose or treat any conditions. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: STAT+: Across the U.S., homegrown experiments aim to save kids from their phones
items.author: Isabella Cueto
items.summary: MILWAUKEE — Kat Zilka sat on the floor of her living room, beside a glowing Christmas tree and a pile of essays, and felt like weeping. It was late in 2022, and she had asked her 12th grade digital journalism students to reflect on their relationships to devices. “The things they were writing were deeply disturbing,” she said. Teenagers quietly enduring online abuse, using their phones all night without their parents’ knowledge, or trapped in a cycle of deleting and redownloading social media. Their words made real what Zilka had been observing for years — how the light in students’ eyes was dimmer, especially since Covid — and revealed the astonishing magnitude of the problem. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on restoring trust in science, the state of public health, and RFK Jr.
items.author: Nicholas Florko
items.summary: Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida , respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000. In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path. Read the rest...

items.title: The Writer Who Made Food Fun
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Sources: Bettmann / Getty; CSA-Printstock / Getty;
items.summary: Before M. F. K. Fisher picked up her pen, most American food writing had a whiff of Victorian fustiness about it—the pinch of the corset. After Fisher, the genre was set free. With an unerring ear for pitch and tone and a mastery of the short-form essay, Fisher inspired multiple generations of writers who might have otherwise never bothered to think rigorously about how and what we eat, and how food can be a source of physical pleasure. Ruth Reichl, Betty Fussell, the Elizabeth Gilbert of Eat Pray Love —all are Fisher’s children. Picador has recently reissued five classic Fisher collections. To reread them is to grasp not only how much joy she infused into food writing but also how much pain she quietly sublimated into her work. Many gastronomists have followed her example; if only more memoirists did too. Fisher herself didn’t have the benefit of clear antecedents. In the decades before her first essay collection, Serve It Forth , was published in 1937, cookbooks enumerated ways for mothers to keep a household running smoothly—the lineaments of what became known as home economics, with the matriarch as a fastidious field general. These books were “stodgy, matter-of-fact, covered v

items.title: The Shamelessness of Marco Rubio
items.author: Colin Hubbard / AP
items.summary: Next to all of the take-Americans-for-nitwits scams perpetrated by the Trump administration, the news that Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been using taxpayer-funded military jets to fly to college-football games doesn’t amount to that much. Still, as evidence of degraded ethics and an emperor-like feed-me-another-grape sensibility, it holds its own. Rubio has defended his flights by saying that the events are important to his family—his son is a senior running back for the Gators. But he’s really Saturday joyriding to big-ticket events, and the message he’s sending is This administration doesn’t serve you. You serve it. Rubio’s son Anthony may be a very nice young man. What he isn’t, arguably, is a college-football player worth flying in to watch—because he barely ever plays. He is a walk-on, a scout-teamer, which means that his primary role is not to play in games but to be a body for his teammates to scrimmage against during practice. It’s a valuable job, from which he’s no doubt learned a lot. But he has made it onto the field for exactly three rushing attempts this season. Yet Rubio, a Florida alum, has flown to at least 10 Gators games. The cost of his personal flights sin

items.title: Zelda ’s Midlife Crisis
items.author: Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic
items.summary: M any video games have reached middle age. Pong did in 2012, Space Invaders in 2018, Pac-Man in 2020. Depending on how nerdy you want to get about provenance, Mario turned 40 in 2021 or 2023 or 2025, and Oregon Trail hit the milestone in 2011 or 2025. Video games, a medium for children that has tried and mostly failed to become sophisticated entertainment for adults, are simply old. The Legend of Zelda , which turned 40 this year, is the latest release at the codger arcade. I am, alas, even older than that. My first encounter with Zelda took place at arm’s length. I had seen the strange television ads for the game, because that is how toys and candy were marketed to children. Despite owning a Nintendo Entertainment System, I felt no pull to play or own the game. It seems idiotic to assert that a fantasy-adventure video game with an elfin boy clad in green struck me as childish, but I could already feel adolescence pulling me from Mario to, well, Maria or her equivalent (who was probably named Jennifer or Heather or Michelle). I vividly remember a conversation with my friend Peter about the game, shortly after its U.S. release in 1987. “Do you ever get tired of Andrew and Peter talk

items.title: The Polls Missed the Blue Tsunami. Why Doesn’t Anyone Care?
items.author: Lakshya Jain
items.summary: (Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/ The Bulwark | Photos: Shutterstock) IN THE WAKE OF THE BLUE TSUNAMI that engulfed America last week, you’ve probably seen some pollsters claiming vindication for the industry. After all, the polls said a blue wave would happen, and it did. The results were proof that, despite the numerous challenges faced by the industry, polling is fine, right? Wrong. I’m not an armchair critic. I am a pollster. Take it from me: The polls did not have a great night. In fact, per data from Matt Grossmann, the director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University, pollsters may have had one of their worst cycles of this century, with a polling miss exceeding the infamous misfires in 2016 and rivaling those of 2020. The reason it’s not being talked about more is because, in 2026, the misfires went in the opposite direction. The polls this cycle undershot Democrats in fourteen of the fifteen key Senate races—all but Nebraska—and often substantially. In North Carolina, Texas, and Georgia, they underestimated the Democratic margin by more than 8 percentage points. The reason the polls missed was entirely predictable: Pollsters w

items.title: NYC Juvenile Lockups Packed Beyond Capacity as Overtime Soars: Report
items.author: Reuven Blau
items.summary: The city’s two juvenile detention centers are operating far beyond capacity, staff overtime has quadrupled and the average length of detention has nearly doubled, according to a new state report. The 69-page review also found that the number of probation officers declined by one-third between 2020 and 2026, even as juvenile caseloads increased. “New York City is spending more money to keep young people in detention, and they are staying there longer,” state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli said in a statement. “The city needs to address staffing shortages and overcrowding and also invest in prevention efforts, including after-school programs, mentoring and summer jobs, to give young people more opportunities and help keep them out of the juvenile justice system.” Overcrowding at the two facilities has gotten so bad the city has been forced to use classroom space as housing units. Earlier this month, a state oversight agency stopped issuing waivers to allow ACS to use those common areas for housing. The report — which covers 2019 through fiscal year 2026 — comes weeks after the Mamdani administration announced a series of changes aimed at addressing problems at the beleaguered facilities

items.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.author: Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.summary: Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

items.title: Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from USA to Manchester United confirmed
items.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer and Will Unwin
items.summary: Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday. The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

items.title: What science can tell us about the art of conversation - video
items.author: Ellie Bury, Ian Sample, Joshan Chana, Jacob Liebenberg, Luke John Smith, Madelei
items.summary: Scientists at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire say they have discovered a telltale sign of an enjoyable conversation. Apparently the secret of a mutually satisfying chat is a healthy dose of pink noise. Guardian science editor Ian Sample tells co-host Madeleine Finlay how this concept usually associated with physics can be applied to conversation, and what the secret to pinkifying our chats could be.

items.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
items.author: Oliver Milman
items.summary: One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades As a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents. The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

items.title: Moscow car bomb severely injures former aide to Ukraine’s pro-Russia ex-PM
items.author: Pjotr Sauer
items.summary: Attack thought to be orchestrated by Kyiv comes day after Russian military official was killed in blast in St Petersburg Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov.

items.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
items.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
items.summary: First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months. “This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

items.title: Let’s talk about Jensen Huang’s many affairs!

Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters. For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions , of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way. Key takeaways This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate. Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024. items.title: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
items.author: Jack Meserve
items.summary: If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball. Next on the list was baseball. The third-most wagered sport? Table tennis. Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier. Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon , the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue. And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling. This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets. And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday. There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting. The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis. It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it. items.title: How Novig became the third biggest prediction market site despite launching only months ago
items.author: Camila Grigera Naón
items.summary: Since bursting on the scene two years ago, prediction markets have become one of the buzziest new sectors in finance, pulling in billions of dollars in revenue, and driving daily news headlines. The young industry is dominated by two giants, Kalshi and Polymarket, but numerous other companies are trying to muscle into the field. That includes the sports-focused prediction market Novig, which only launched as a federally regulated prediction market in August, but has already claimed the number three spot by one widely used industry metric. Over the past 30 days, Novig handled $1.8 billion in trading volume on U.S.-regulated exchanges, according to the PM Pulse, a newsletter that tracks prediction market volume using data from research firm Aldrin. That figure is small next to Kalshi’s $33.3 billion and Polymarket U.S.’s $6.3 billion. But it’s about $300 million ahead of Crypto.com, the fourth-place contender, and its volume is up 80% from the previous 30 days. The volume figures don’t account for combos, or multi-game parlays, which Sam Schwartz, who runs the newsletter, says can inflate volume without producing proportionally more revenue for the exchange. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir. On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies , made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit. Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Reality is on our side From Brazil to Hungary and Britain to the US, why are so many people so surprised by the right’s election defeats? Flávio Bolsonaro, Viktor Orbán, Reform UK, the Tories and a vast array of Republican candidates have all been rejected in national or local contests this year, even in usually reliably conservative Mississippi. Apparently impregnable incumbents and populist insurgents alike have been beaten, often by big margins . The supposedly ascendant global right has been out-organised, out-thought, outmanoeuvred and outnumbered. Yet each time this happens – which is more often than the usual gloomy narrative of our politics allows – many liberals and leftists absorb and share the good news almost with wonderment . The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though. The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

items.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

items.title: Cancer vaccines show promise for treatment and prevention
items.summary: For more than three decades, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have pursued an ambitious idea: that vaccines could train the immune system to recognize and fight cancer. Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

items.title: Key brain area reveals distinct zones whose boundaries blur with age
items.author: Leah Eisenstadt
items.summary: Scientists in the Center for Human Brain Variation at the Broad Institute have charted previously hidden architecture and patterns of cellular makeup in a key part of the brain called the striatum, which is involved in decision-making and movement and is affected in psychiatric disorders, addiction and neurodegeneration. The findings reveal six new zones within the striatum based on gene expression patterns. They also demonstrate how the zones' boundaries blur with age and highlight ways that advancing age and genetic variation affect gene expression in the brain.

items.title: Molecular mapping of 8 million cells brings cerebral architecture into focus

The work offers a foundational reference for investigating brain systems affected by Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

items.title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
items.author: Beth Mole
items.summary: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. items.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
items.summary: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

items.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search

items.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. items.title: AI-powered lung cancer atlas identifies cell types linked to higher risk of spread
items.summary: Recent advances in cancer biology have shown that a tumor is not a uniform mass. It consists of many different cancer cells and is embedded in an environment of immune cells, connective tissue and blood vessels. This variety is a significant factor in determining whether a tumor spreads and how well a therapy works. While single-cell approaches are considered pioneering instruments in cancer research, their translation into clinical practice has been limited to date, primarily due to a lack of large patient data sets with comprehensive clinical histories.

items.title: What spaceflight reveals about nerves and bone recovery

The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

On Tuesday, a judge placed Michel Houellebecq, one of the country’s most significant living writers, under investigation for his alleged “complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence,” an accusation that stems from comments he made about Muslims several years ago. Houellebecq’s remarks were controversial and insensitive, but defending his freedom to speak does not require finding his words unobjectionable. Even the most offensive generalizations about minority groups should have to meet an exceptionally high threshold to warrant such a legal intervention. Houellebecq’s do not. The fact that he now faces the possibility of criminal charges should concern anyone who professes to care about the free exchange of ideas. items.author: Benjamin Fanjoy / Getty
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia, following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese-intelligence asset, should force a fundamental rethinking of America’s AI strategy. Jensen Huang was not just the CEO of the world’s most important semiconductor company. He was also one of Donald Trump’s closest and most influential advisers on AI. Huang persuaded Trump to abandon his initial embrace of export controls, arguing that U.S. technology firms should compete in China. He persistently argued that AI is more akin to electricity than a weapon and that warnings about AI safety were wildly overblown—a view that Trump fully internalized. In the coming months, Congress will scrutinize every aspect of the scandal. Among these are the Commerce Department’s suspension of its investigation into Megaspeed, the Singaporean company that Alice Huang was a director of; the failure to crack down on China’s extensive chip-smuggling operation in Southeast Asia; Nvidia’s financial contributions to Trump’s pet projects, such as the White House ballroom; and China’s possible illicit influence over other business leaders in America

The story, set in Brooklyn and Queens in the 1980s, manages to be both tightly focused and operatic in scale: Two brothers (played by Adam Driver and Miles Teller) get in over their heads on a business scheme, and must watch as their dream of climbing the social ladder is brutally ripped away—partly thanks to their own mistakes. items.title: How a warming ocean is changing the base of the marine food web
items.summary: Climate change is causing warming in the oceans, which can have significant effects on marine food webs. Rising ocean temperatures can intensify seawater stratification, a process in which ocean water forms layers of different densities that mix less readily. This can reduce the supply of nutrients to surface waters and favor smaller phytoplankton species that are better adapted to low-nutrient conditions. Phytoplankton support zooplankton, which in turn transfer energy to fish and other animals. Changes in phytoplankton communities can therefore lead to cascading effects on marine food webs.

items.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
items.author: Nathan Bomey
items.summary: Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself . Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. items.title: The disturbing reality behind America’s milk and cheese — and the fight to end it
items.author: Marina Bolotnikova
items.summary: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare. Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it. At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies . Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef. items.title: The Guardian view on Gaza’s misery: don’t let Palestinian deaths mount in this bleak winter | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals , which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared. The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. Israeli military personnel have also described the shockingly high level of civilian deaths tolerated as “collateral damage” in targeting even low-level fighters after the brutal Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.

items.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry. The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

items.title: Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
items.author: Beth Mole
items.summary: For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way. But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it's primarily used to beef up cows. Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week's issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like. Read full article Comments

items.title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
items.author: John Timmer
items.summary: One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet's atmosphere. Except when we can't. On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we've been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that's due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane. Read full article Comments

Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a "simple" rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, "the best part is no part." Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket's development cycle. "Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines," he said of the rocket. "So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite." Read full article Comments

items.title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.summary: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Read full article Comments

items.summary: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA). At that point, Nvidia sported the world’s biggest market cap at $5.85 trillion. Wall Street analysts following the stock were almost universal even then in acclaiming Nvidia as a cheap stock. items.title: Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy: ‘An advantage for us’

Speaking at a media roundtable, Bill Winters said the splintering of global trade is creating new business for the bank, which helps multinational corporations manage cross-border deals, the South China Morning Post reported . His remarks come as companies rethink where they make things amid rising trade tensions. Many have adopted a “China plus one” strategy, shifting some production to Southeast Asia to offset China’s rising costs. That shift has proven more complicated than expected, as many factories in the region still rely on Chinese inputs, Fortune reported in October . Why a fractured economy is good business for Standard Chartered Geopolitical fragmentation refers to the structural shift in the global economy as supply chains, trade, and policy realign along political lines. items.title: ‘The plot twist’: A study of 73,000 adults found America’s richest still die sooner than most Europeans
items.author: Lena Borrelli
items.summary: Americans have never earned more or lived longer. Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967, according to Census data released in September . Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record . Yet money still can’t buy Americans a European lifespan. A Brown University study published last year in the New England Journal of Medicine found that Americans die sooner than Europeans at every level of wealth, and that the richest Americans fare no better than the poorest people in much of Western Europe. “The plot twist is that even the wealthiest quartile of Americans does not have better outcomes than most of northern and Western Europeans,” says Sara Machado, a research scientist at Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. “That was unexpected and counters a lot of the narrative that we’re used to.” What the Brown study found The researchers tracked more than 73,000 adults ages 50 to 85 in the U.S. and 16 European countries, starting in 2010 and following them for about a decade, using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study and Europe’s SHARE survey. items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

items.title: American Cancer Society updates prostate cancer screening guideline: Regular PSA testing for average- and high-risk men
items.summary: The American Cancer Society (ACS) today released an updated guideline for prostate cancer screening to help find cancer before it spreads and reduce the risk of dying from the disease. Key changes include a direct recommendation for prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening every two years for average-risk men aged 50–69, with clinicians ensuring patients understand the potential benefits, limitations and harms before starting screening. Also, ACS recommends annual PSA-based screening beginning at 45 years old for Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer.

items.title: Cell changes around early breast cancers provide clues to why some cases become invasive
items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have created one of the most detailed maps to date of the cell environment surrounding ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), the most common form of preinvasive, or stage 0, breast cancer. The findings may help explain why some lesions progress to invasive breast cancer and others do not, informing strategies to improve patient risk prediction and develop better targeted approaches for patients at higher risk of invasive disease.

items.title: First complete genomes for neglected malaria parasites revealed
items.summary: Scientists have produced gold-standard reference genomes for previously neglected malaria parasites by sequencing low-input DNA directly from patient blood, bypassing lab culture.

items.title: New guidelines recommend regular prostate cancer screening for all middle-aged men
items.summary: Experts now recommend regular prostate cancer screening for all men ages 50 to 69 and earlier for higher-risk groups, according to new American Cancer Society (ACS) guidelines.

items.title: Inflammation is involved in the earliest stages of atherosclerosis
items.summary: Inflammation plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis from its earliest stages, long before the onset of symptoms or cardiovascular events such as heart attack or stroke. This is the main conclusion of a study led by a team at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) and published in the European Heart Journal. The research shows that systemic inflammation contributes to disease development independently of traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as elevated cholesterol and hypertension.

items.title: Mice help researchers discover how the COVID virus triggers sneezing and coughing
items.summary: In the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, as Diana Bautista and others in her UC Berkeley lab suffered sneezing and coughing fits and achy bodies, she asked an interesting scientific question: How, exactly, do viruses cause the noxious symptoms we're all familiar with from bouts with colds, the flu and COVID?

items.title: Smelling Parkinson's: From discovery to skin swab test
items.summary: A retired nurse who noticed that people with Parkinson's had a distinct odor inspired Manchester scientists to explore changes in molecules on the skin's surface. Using a simple skin swab, they can detect about 15,000 molecular features, approximately 10% of which consistently differ in abundance between people with and without Parkinson's.

items.title: Surveyed cancer patients say cannabis improves symptoms
items.summary: A new study by the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center and the Kentucky Cannabis Center provides insight into how some cancer patients are using cannabis, the benefits they report and how physicians can help patients make informed decisions.

items.title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
items.summary: Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

items.title: Holiday Extras is rethinking what it can build with Codex
items.summary: With Codex, Holiday Extras is turning customer expertise into better apps, higher booking conversion and new possibilities for growth.

items.title: Supporting research on AI and children’s safety
items.summary: OpenAI commits $2 million to research on AI and children’s safety. The work supports shared tools to measure risks and opportunities for young people.

items.title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI
items.summary: A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

items.title: New analytical method offers potential for faster risk assessment of avian influenza viruses
items.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza causes significant damage to the poultry industry worldwide. As the virus evolves, new variants regularly emerge that may differ in how easily they spread and how severely they affect infected birds. Researchers at Wageningen Bioveterinary Research (WBVR, part of Wageningen University & Research) characterized eight avian influenza virus variants in chicken and duck cells. Using mathematical modeling, they identified differences in how these viruses behave in poultry cells. Their paper is published in Microbiology Spectrum.

items.title: From bush food to biodegradable materials: Unlocking the potential of pigface
items.author: Cecilia Duong
items.summary: An Australian native plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities for food and medicine could help scientists develop stronger, more flexible biodegradable film. UNSW researchers have discovered that adding extracts from pigface, Carpobrotus glaucescens, a hardy coastal succulent, to seaweed-based films can significantly improve their strength and flexibility.

items.title: Chemical traces hint at poisoned hunting weapons in Arabia 125,000 years ago
items.summary: A new study has found people living in Arabia 125,000 years ago used complex technologies, including composite hunting weapons, plant-fiber processing and possibly poison-assisted hunting, while making use of a freshwater lake rich in resources.

items.title: The diamond paradox: Scientists describe the path to the most stable structure
items.summary: Researchers from Skoltech (part of the VEB.RF Group) and MISIS University have figured out why graphite turns into an unexpected form of diamond under high pressure. Instead of the familiar cubic diamond, the first structure to form is metastable lonsdaleite—a hexagonal form of diamond in which carbon atoms are arranged in layers differently than in ordinary diamond.

items.title: Electron beam tests advance safer sterilization method for flies that threaten livestock
items.author: Adam Russell
items.summary: Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists have achieved early success using electron beam, or eBeam, technology for the sterile insect technique, or SIT, against New World screwworm flies.

items.title: Elephants found to be increasingly isolated, leading to fractured social networks
items.summary: Humans and many other social animals thrive in well-established community networks. Asian elephants are one example of a species that flourishes in groups that work together to access food and care for their young, among other social bonds.

items.title: Why teaching 'ethical' classroom use of AI to learn writing must include the right to refuse
items.summary: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in "ethical" ways—for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI?

items.title: Euclid offers best-ever 3D map of the universe to date
items.summary: The Euclid Consortium and the European Space Agency (ESA) have released the first major batch of data from the Euclid space telescope. This release, which captures light from more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky equivalent to 9,500 full moons, lays the foundation for Europe's dark universe detective's largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos. Several German research facilities play crucial roles in the Euclid mission's success.

items.title: Unified framework establishes rules for classifying unconventional magnets
items.summary: Researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a unified framework for establishing symmetry criteria and classifying unconventional magnets.

items.title: High water, high rents: Poorest residents pay the most for climate adaptation
items.summary: As cities worldwide adapt to extreme weather, climate adaptation must prevent people from wading through flooded streets in the future. But the costs are not equally shared. A study from the University of Copenhagen shows that climate adaptation policies may even make social inequality worse. In Copenhagen, stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, as these neighborhoods are often located near climate adaptation projects.

items.title: How human ideas evolve: Technical progress may not require weeding out weaker designs
items.summary: Human culture evolves similarly to living organisms, but unlike biology, human creativity can accumulate improvements at an incredible speed. But how exactly does the process of transmitting and modifying ideas between people work?

items.title: Large mutation analysis challenges claim that evolution shields important genes from changes
items.summary: The idea that important genes mutate less frequently than others was first proposed in 1972 as a challenge to the traditional view of evolution. But the claim has remained contentious. Now, new research from the University of Bath finds the evidence behind that theory to be flawed.

items.title: Lipids from banana peels help cherry tomatoes stay fresh longer
items.summary: Fruits and vegetables keep "breathing" even after they're picked. Respiration consumes sugars and organic acids that contribute to flavor, while moisture loss and continued ripening soften the fruit. These changes shorten shelf life and contribute to food waste. Thin edible coatings can be applied to regulate gas and water transfer and preserve fresh produce. Now, food scientists are exploring whether byproducts we often discard could supply ingredients for these coatings.

items.title: A new twist on 'magic-angle' graphene: Tuning resistance with strain
items.summary: In materials science labs around the world, researchers regularly reproduce a peculiar experiment. Under a microscope, they use tiny robotic manipulators to lay two sheets of carbon, each a single atom thick, against one another. They then rotate the top sheet against the bottom. The two identical lattices of atoms, when twisted relative to one another, bloom into a complex moiré pattern, a shifting complex of honeycomb shapes that grow and shrink as the angle between the layers changes.

items.title: Study finds midlife women face unique need for workplace flexibility
items.summary: New research from the Working for Women Research Partnership (WFWRP) shows overlapping life demands make women ages 40–55 more likely than other groups to both want and need workplace flexibility.

items.title: Nitrate pollution in rivers linked to dry climates, not just human activity
items.summary: Nitrate, a chemical compound of oxygen and nitrogen often used in farm fertilizers, can rise to toxic levels in surrounding water under very dry conditions. This relationship has traditionally been attributed to agricultural runoff or human waste in the environment, but new research led by scientists at Penn State shows that a hot and dry climate elevates concentrations of nitrate in rivers and streams, even in areas without urban or agricultural development.

items.title: Rain may increase ocean carbon uptake more than we thought
items.summary: Global carbon budgets, which track carbon's movement among the atmosphere, ocean and land, may underestimate how much carbon the ocean absorbs by roughly 5% to 15% because current estimates do not fully account for rain's effects on the ocean surface.

items.title: Feeling pressured to be grateful? Don't force it
items.summary: It's that time of year when gratitude seems to be everywhere: at work, around the dinner table and at holiday gatherings. But with so much pressure to feel thankful, gratitude can start to feel like one more thing on the holiday to-do list.

items.title: Finding romance with AI: Study explores benefits, limits of chatbot intimacy
items.author: Noor Hindi
items.summary: An AI companion can be available for a late-night conversation, respond to personal disclosures and discuss a favorite topic for hours. For people who develop intimate relationships with chatbots, those exchanges can offer a meaningful sense of connection.

items.title: Seaweeds can switch to asexual reproduction when there are no mates nearby
items.summary: Kelp switch between sexual and asexual reproduction depending on whether there are potential mates nearby, according to a study by Daniel Liesner at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany, and colleagues, published Nov. 12 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology.

items.title: Sensors track stress in plants in real time—without hurting them in the process
items.summary: Even plants, from towering palm trees to vegetables such as onions and eggplants, can get stressed. Now, a team of engineers has designed a new kind of sensor that attaches directly to plants and peers inside them to track how they respond to stressors such as drought and fires in real time.

items.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
items.summary: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time.

items.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
items.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust.

items.title: Tiny cracks and a 9-volt battery could help fight deadly superbugs
items.summary: As superbugs become harder to treat and antibiotic resistance continues to rise worldwide, Flinders University scientists have uncovered an unlikely ally in the fight to prevent infections before they take hold. They have found that carefully controlled microscopic cracks can enhance the performance of an antibacterial coating, which helps destroy dangerous bacteria when activated with a small electrical charge.

items.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
items.author: Sarahbeth Maney
items.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans. In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.” It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.” But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office. They are not just numbers. Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday. Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica. Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In their own neighbor

items.title: Pentagon, Inc.
items.author: Rebecca Gordon
items.summary: Self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment for “high crimes and misdemeanors” on Tuesday. That failed effort sets Hegseth up for a reckoning in the new year. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. And many Democrats — fresh off an electoral rout of the GOP — are spoiling for a fight. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted. They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept on Tuesday. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it. It didn’t work. We’ll do it again.” A mountain of evidence is poised to fall on Hegseth’s head. He could be convicted of countless crimes. But just because Congress has a government official dead to rights doesn’t mean that that official won’t evade justice. items.title: OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official
items.author: Sam Biddle
items.summary: A Russian internet comedy duo tricked three of OpenAI’s highest ranking military and national security staff into a candid conversation about arming Ukraine. The online pranksters posed as officials from Ukraine’s government, according to a recording of the meeting posted online. The Russian comedy duo known as Vovan and Lexus have pulled off a long string of prank telephone calls to famous figures since 2011, with victims ranging from Elton John to John McCain. The group, whose pranks have often aligned with Russian foreign policy priorities, have been accused of working in league with its government , a charge they deny. Related AI Tried to Buy the Midterms — Then the Lobby Learned Everyone Hates AI The latest to fall for their routine were Sasha Baker, who runs national security policy at OpenAI; the company’s lead for strategic initiatives, Caroline Zier; and Ben Crampton, who leads the company’s forays into European national security matters.
